utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Before you begin, Mr. Mandic, I hope you have enjoyed the summer in the Netherlands over the weekend. Recalling your statement that you had difficulty when you entered the Netherlands at Schiphol with the [indiscernible] having to wait for you for about an hour, the Chamber asked the Registry to look into the matter, and I believe the VWS, the Victim and Witnesses Section, will explain the situation to you in due course. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, just before we adjourned on Thursday, you were asked about the report on the activities in the Ministry of Justice and Administration in the period May through October 1992, and you indicated that you had -- you said: "I cannot give answers in relation to something that happened before me, that is to say, before the Ministry of Justice was established." And you've previously indicated you were appointed on or about the 12th of May, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to look at, actually, when you first became aware that you would be minister of justice and how quickly you or other representatives of the Ministry of Justice began to work. And in that connection, I wanted to turn your attention to page 9366 of your testimony in Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I can answer your question straight away. I was invited to one of the meetings of the Security Council. It was a co-ordinating body. I don't know what its function was. It was the end of April. I think it was the 24th or the 26th of April. And during that part of the session when nominations were being made, that is to say, when information was being provided to certain physical persons, I was called in, too, and I was informed that Rajko Nikolic, the first minister of justice of the Republika Srpska, or, rather, the Republic of the Serb people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who was appointed to the Ministerial Council, had not reported to his job, and then I was informed that I would be minister of justice and that I should prepare everything and take all necessary action in order to prepare for that job or, rather, to take over that ministry; that is to say that on the 24th and 26th of April, I was informed about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off while the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And during the course of your testimony in the Krajisnik case, at pages, approximately, 8727 through 8730, you had an opportunity to look at a May 1st, 1992, letter to the presidents of district assemblies, which you indicated was your effort to begin the establishment of the organs of the Ministry of Justice. Do you recall that, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So shortly after you were advised that you were to assume the position of minister of justice, you began undertaking efforts to establish the ministry?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as that written communication was concerned, 15 days -- it happened 15 days after I was informed that I would be minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic. Now, on Friday we had looked at a session of the National Security Council on April 24th, 1992. We had looked at the establishment of the Exchange Commission on 8 May, 1992, and the document signed by Mr. Markovic on the 14th of May, reflecting the work of the Exchange Commission. I'd like to turn next to a document dated 6 June 1992. That's 65 ter 11024. As the English version of this document is coming up, Mr. Mandic, let me indicate to the Court that this is an order from the Central Commission of the Serbian Republic of BH for exchange of prisoners of War, Detainees, and Bodies of the killed that are on the territory of the opposite side. And it's signed by the president of the commission, Rajko Colovic. Now, Mr. Mandic, first of all, you're familiar with this document; correct? You've had an opportunity to see it before and discuss it before?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first saw this order when I spoke to you and during the trial of Mr. Momo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's look at a few provisions of that order, if we can. The first part of the order indicates that the employees of the Public Security Services, engaged in safe-guarding facilities where prisoners of war or detainees are located, shall keep evidence; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we look down to the third paragraph, there's a reference to the fact that municipal commissions for exchange shall submit lists to regional commissions for exchange, if any, or to the central commission. And that's a reflection of the parametal structure of the Exchange Commission that you explained in the Krajisnik case; is that right? That is, that there were exchange commissions in municipalities at regional levels and a central commission at the republic level; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct. Actually, Mr. Tieger, during the beginning of the war, as far as I know, first it was municipal commissions that were set up, that is to say, for the exchange of prisoners of war and others mentioned in this order. This was done on the basis of crisis staffs and municipal authorities on the ground. In the effort made by the government to centralise this commission and to establish law and order, a central commission was set up for the exchange of prisoners of war at the level of the government, and it was the government that passed a decision to establish this commission. It consisted of representatives of individual ministries who were professionally eligible for that job.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, can I ask you to turn to the second page in B/C/S, and that would be approximately the third paragraph on your page. And at page 3 in English, Your Honours, the fourth paragraph, we find the reference I wanted to draw Mr. Mandic's attention to. That provides as follows, Mr. Mandic: "All women whose detention or deprivation of liberty is not related to the war or war activities, all the children and minors up to 16 years of age, old and helpless persons, shall be released immediately and ensure their return according to their own free will without setting any conditions to them or exchanging them." Now, again, Mr. Mandic, you had an opportunity both to see and provide feedback on that provision in the course of the Krajisnik case, and is it, therefore, correct that the provision providing that women whose deprivation of liberty is not related to the war or war activities does the not apply to men of military age; that is, the release of people whose activities are not related to the war applies only to women, children, minors, old, and helpless persons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, indeed, as you indicated to the Court during the course of the Krajisnik case, the Exchange Commission was involved in the exchange of civilians?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the commission was involved in the exchange of persons who had been taken prisoner, not civilians, all persons who were in specific facilities of the territory of Republika Srpska or the federation. So a mutual exchange was carried out on the basis of an agreement reached between political and state leaderships of the republic or, rather, the federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, at page 8758 of the Krajisnik testimony, Mr. Mandic, you were asked about that issue. You indicated, at page 8757, as the discussion began with questions from the Court about persons who had been detained, either taken into custody as combatants and so on, whereas the others might be civilians or whatever -- that's at page 8757 through 8758. Then you were asked: "If you say 'civilians,' what civilians do you have in mind?" This is at page 8758: " ... civilians under suspicion of having committed offences or just civilians?" And you said: "Both." Then you were asked by the Judge: "And they were deprived --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please ask the distinguished Mr. Tieger to read the entire paragraph to the witness so that things are not taken into -- out of context yet again and presented in a piecemeal fashion?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm obviously reading extensively. If there's any context to be provided beyond that, it can either be provided by Mr. Mandic or by the accused during his examination. But I don't think there's any problem with context in this case, as I'm explaining it and reading it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read some other parts? I haven't -- do we have that paragraph before us, 8757? No, not yet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, I remember very well the conversation I had with His Honour Judge Orie, to whom I tried to explain certain things and I tried to analyse certain things, although I was not familiar with the work of that commission and I did not take part in the work of that commission in any way. This interpretation of what a civilian person is and who a prisoner of war is and who a prisoner is, that is clearly specified in the instructions provided by the minister of defence in June 1992, on the basis of the order issued by the president of the republic, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. Now, this order, this order issued by that commission, why does it in a way confuse laws and regulations in that area? Because until then there was no written document that provided for the treatment of such persons and how they should be treated; that is to say, the state authorities of Republika Srpska had not believed until then that there would be a war and that persons of non-Serb ethnicity would be taken prisoner. From this -- from this order, that is, we can see that Mr. Colovic, who was assistant minister, assistant minister of justice, so he was assistant minister to Mr. Ranko Nikolic, as far as criminal sanctions are concerned, he applied the provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure of the former SFRY and also the Law on Regular Courts that prescribed how persons who are detained should be treated. It's not prisoners of war, but detainees. That is where there is this clash between certain provisions of the two respective laws. That was regulated during the month of June by the order mentioned a few moments ago and also the instructions provided by the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You answered before you heard the question put by Mr. Tieger. But was that answer satisfactory to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I add something, because I'm a Court witness. Mr. Rajko Colovic was never an employee of the Ministry of Justice of Republika Srpska. By applying the provisions of the Law on Regular Courts that stipulate that the president of a relevant court, or a judge authorised by him, are duty-bound to visit all persons who are detained every 14 days to see how their condition is, how they're being treated, and in certain cases they should inform the Ministry of Justice about that. Mr. Rajko Colovic took over those previsions from the pre-war laws and he wrote them up in this order. Obviously, this order is not adequate in relation to these laws or, rather, the Law on Criminal Procedure of the SFRY and the Law on Regular Courts. For wont of certain provisions, Mr. Colovic wrote up this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to clarify further, Mr. Mandic, I was referring to your testimony in the Krajisnik case. Again, Judge Orie asked: "If you say 'civilians,' what civilians do you have in mind; civilians under suspicion of having committed offences or just civilians?" And your answer was: "Both, as long as they weren't involved in any armed conflict, in armed combat, and so on in the war, that they weren't apprehended with weapons, that they hadn't taken part in armed conflicts, in fighting, or anything like that." And then the Judge asked: "And they were deprived their liberty on the basis of what?" And you answered: "I really can't say, Your Honour, because this was done by the Security Services employees and the army." And the Judge asked: "Yes, but it was part of the exchange, I think. As far as I understood, representatives of your ministry were involved in the exchange of prisoners, of the exchange of detained persons?" And you answered: "Yes, detained civilians." That's correct, isn't it? That's what you explained to the Judge at the time he was asking you about the Exchange Commission?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I tried, on the basis of my own knowledge, to explain to His Honour Judge Orie, from my own point of view, what the definition of a civilian person is, also my knowledge as to how these persons had reached premises that were envisaged for detention. Now, whether they were taken prisoner by the army or some other armed formations, that is something I did not know, or whether these were persons who were being taken away from places where there was an armed conflict, as was the case with Dobrinja. It's not a question of taking persons prisoner, but giving them shelter while there is an armed conflict going on, so that they could be taken back or taken somewhere else later. I tried to explain, on the basis of my own experience, what the definition of a civilian was. I did not participate in this, and I did not have any knowledge as to how these persons had reached these premises that crisis staffs or other authorities had appointed as detention facilities for these persons. After all, those who interrogated and detained these persons knew whether they were civilians or participants in armed conflict. That's the Territorial Defence, the army, and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let's turn next to a session of the government on the 9th of June, 1992. That's 65 ter 00172. And this reflects a session of the government just a few days after the Colovic order. And if you'll cast your eye on agenda item number 1(a), it states that the government has supported order of the Central Commission for the exchange of prisoners. And that would be a reference to the 6 June Colovic order; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic. And, Your Honour, before I get too far behind, I should note that I need to tender this document as well as the previous two, which would include 65 ter 16249, the May through October Ministry of Justice report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 65 ter number, is it not 11024 that you used previously?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, and that's my fault for letting us get behind. So the three documents that need to be tendered at this point are the document currently before us, the 9 June government session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I noted 16249 was the one which was used in the previous session last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You haven't tendered that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that's right. So it would be that document, then, the 6 June Exchange Commission order we just looked at a moment ago, and now the 9 June government session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Unless they are objected to, they will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 16249 will be Exhibit P1089. 65 ter 11024 will be Exhibit P1090. And 65 ter 00172 will be Exhibit P1091.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, if we can next turn to a government session the very next day, 10 June 1992, and that's 65 ter 00173. And with the assistance of the Registry, if we could turn to page 3 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Tieger. This is a different document. This is minutes from a different government session, not the one that you had showed earlier on. Have we finished dealing with that government session where the order of the Central Commission was adopted?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I've moved on to the session the next day, Mr. Mandic. It sounds like you want to make a comment on the 9th June session.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't let me allow -- you didn't let me explain. Yes, yes, yes, I did not attend that government session. No one from the Ministry of Justice attended that session. So I became aware of these government decisions during June 1992, a couple of days later. If you go back to the beginning of this document, you will see that I did not attend this session, and no one else from the Ministry of Justice did, and that is where the nominations took place as far as members of the Central Commission are concerned. That was the session of the 9th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's focus our attention, as I suggested, for the moment on the 10th of June session, which I believe is still before you. And you were in attendance at that session; correct, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at agenda item 7 under "Current Issues," the following conclusions were made: "That the Ministry of Justice should make a report about prisoners. This report should pay special attention on treatment of civilian population, prisoners of war, accommodation, food, et cetera. The report would be considered by the government, after which it would be submitted to the Presidency of the republic." Now, Mr. Mandic, you were asked about this government session during the course of your testimony in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case, and at page 9492 you indicated -- or you testified that this situation, that is, the conclusion that a report should be made, arose because there had been complaints about the treatment of the civilian population, in particular: "Q. We see here that the Ministry of Justice should make a report about prisoners, the report should pay special attention on the treatment of the civilian population, prisoners of war, accommodation, food, et cetera, and the report would be considered by the government, after which it would be submitted to the Presidency. Now, did that arise because there had been complaints about the treatment of the civilian population in particular?" And your answer: "Yes, yes."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information reached us from the field about certain instances of the inhuman treatment of detained persons. Whether they were POWs or civilians, I cannot remember. In an attempt to establish the rule of law, the government took steps to co-ordinate the work of the commissions and to have some specialists from the Ministry of Justice, from the Ministry of the Police, of the Interior, and from other departments to go out in the field to report to the government about the actual situation in the field, and the government was to inform all the competent institutions, the Presidency, the Assembly, and, of course, the government about that situation so that urgent steps could be taken to overcome the situation and to prevent any further violations of the 1949 Geneva Conventions. Everything that is written here was undertaken by the ministry. A commission was set up. It went out in the field, it surveyed the situation, it wrote up a report, and informed the government and the competent institutions about the situation as found.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would have been helpful if we heard the whole paragraph. I should just like to say that we should read the entire paragraph, because just a part of it was quoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the witness remembered the situation clearly, and he had no difficulty at all in answering the question. Then it is for you to supplement during your cross-examination. Please refrain from intervening in such a way during the Prosecution's examination. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asked, in cross-examination, when I quoted something, that I should quote it in full rather than interpret or summarise text, so I'm just following the instructions given me when I was doing the examining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I agree with that principle, but I didn't see any problem with Mr. Tieger examination. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And furthermore, Your Honour, the entirety of this transcript is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. We have, as evidence, the Stanisic transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is from the -- oh, I apologise, Your Honour. You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have nothing against its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, the conclusion that we've just looked at indicates that the report would be considered by the government, after which it would be submitted to the Presidency of the republic. Do you recall who or which body initiated the inquiry about the issue of the treatment of civilian population, prisoners of war, accommodation, food, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember who it was. I know that Mr. Djeric informed us about the information that he had received, and the prime minister, of course, and these conclusions were adopted at his initiative, at his proposal. Who the actual proponent was, I cannot recall. Mr. Branko Djeric would be able to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to look at another official record of an official body on that same date of 10 June 1992, and that's the minutes of the 5th Session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, held during an imminent threat of war on 10 June 1992. And that's 65 ter 00115. And I want to look, in particular, at two portions of those minutes, both at the beginning and the end. As you'll see, Mr. Mandic, at the beginning of the session, just below the indication of the persons who were present, the minutes indicate that at the beginning of the session, the Presidency reviewed information received during night on the situation at the front and reports of the international public or foreign press. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then if we turn to the second page of the English and also the second page of the B/C/S, in the second-to-last paragraph it indicates, with respect to Dr. Branko Djeric, that: "The government submit a report on prisoners, with proposed measures."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exactly consistent with what I just said, that Branko Djeric conveyed this information to us and charged specific persons to go out in the field and to inspect the situation, in the field and in the facilities where non-Serbs were being detained, and to submit a report on that. So non-Serbs. As a rule, the members of the government got all their information from Mr. Djeric, who was both a member of the Supreme Command and of the Presidency, and he was one of the best-informed people in 1992 in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Together with the previous document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the first time in my life that I see this document. I have not had occasion to see it before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I don't think there's any objection to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both documents will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 00173 will be Exhibit P1092, and 65 ter 00115 will be P1093.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, as noted a moment ago, at the beginning of the session, according to the minutes, the Presidency reviewed reports of the international public or foreign press. Were you aware at that time of allegations from the international community or international media about the detention of non-Serb civilians by Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All my information derived from the information imparted to us at government sessions by the prime minister, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that connection, did Mr. Djeric advise you and the other members of government of allegations by the international community, the international media, or others from -- connected with the international public about the detention of non-Serbs by Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. This is information about the positions of the international community. It is not stated anywhere that their positions were on prisons, which Mr. Tieger is implying. We assist everything which was happening in the international community regarding the conference, the end of the war, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the question was put to the witness. If you wish to give testimony, we will welcome you. The witness will answer the question as far as he knows and as far as he remembers. It's not for you to intervene, Mr. Karadzic. I find it very unhelpful, Mr. Karadzic. Yes. Have you finished your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I can recap it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I had asked you if you were aware of allegations by the international community whether -- international organisations, international public, international media, concerning the detention of non-Serbs by Bosnian Serb authorities. I believe you answered that you got your information from Mr. Djeric, so I asked you if Mr. Djeric imparted to you such information; that is --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not about that, no, Mr. Tieger. I didn't say that he informed us about that. He informed us about the situation in the field, and the events in the field were reported to us by Mr. Djeric at government sessions. I had no contact whatsoever, nor any information did I receive from the international public or the media. All the information from the sessions of the Presidency or any body in the leadership of the Republika Srpska were conveyed to us at government sessions by Mr. Djeric; not only on this issue, but on any problems which cropped up in the course of the creation of the state, i.e., Republika Srpska. As you can see from the minutes here, the government reacted to such information, i.e., to proposals by Mr. Djeric for steps to be taken in order to establish the rule of law and ensure the safety -- the security of those people who were of non-Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And we can take a quick look, then, at 65 ter 05991. Mr. Mandic, I'm going to ask you to look at a letter from Dr. Djeric, dated, I believe, the 24th of May, 1992, to Mr. James Baker, the US secretary of state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in it, as we can see at the very beginning of the document, Mr. Djeric appears to be responding to what he calls the most disturbing news, suggesting the possible use of force against what he calls the Serbian population in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then he proceeds, in the course of that letter, to address a number of issues. And if you'll look, please, at the fifth paragraph in English, which is located on the first page of your document as well, Dr. Djeric states: "You can rest assured that Serbian side is holding no hostages, operating no concentration camps, and is not killing unarmed civilians in Bosnia. The reports alleging such crimes, appearing in the US press and elsewhere, are not based on facts." And then he continues discussing demographics, entitlement to land, the genocide of World War II, and so on. Now, Mr. Mandic, I take it that you'll agree that this is a reflection of the fact that there were allegations or Dr. Djeric's concern about allegations in the international press and by the international community concerning, among other issues, the existence of concentration camps in which non-Serb civilians were detained?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time, Mr. Tieger, that I see this letter. I'm not a court expert. I cannot comment on Mr. Djeric's letter from the expert side. I do not agree with you that Mr. Djeric was concerned about a possible NATO attack on the Serb people, but I think that he wrote a letter which fell within his competence, as it were, to the international mediator, Mr. Baker, to present to him his view of the war in May 1992. I don't know anything about the content of this letter. I'm not an analysis expert, so I cannot comment on the letter, itself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Is the 65 ter number correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told it's 951. Oh, yes, thank you. Just 5991 instead of 951.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I misspoke, Your Honour, I apologise, but it seemed to come under the number I indicated previously. But maybe there's a slip between the reading and the enunciation. But you're correct about the number, and the correct document is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'm not asking you to analyse the document. The document speaks for itself. I'm asking you whether or not you claim you were completely unaware of any concern among the members of the Bosnian Serb leadership about reports or allegations from the international community concerning concentration camps or detention facilities maintained by the Bosnian Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not the way it is, Mr. Tieger. All his concerns that Mr. Djeric presented at the government sessions, and the information which came from the field, was something that the government reacted to by setting up these commissions which would go out in the field to inspect the situation and to remedy the situation, to have the existing camps comply with the International Convention -- with the provisions of the International Convention on Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We've just looked a moment ago at -- and, sorry, Your Honour. If I haven't tendered that letter, I'd like to do so now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we are to follow a principle, the witness confirmed nothing about the document, so we'll admit it at a later stage if you use it with the proper witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't -- I'm going to say -- okay, let me reiterate the concern I expressed on Thursday about documents and document admissibility and falling within the guide-lines. I think this document naturally arises from what was raised by the previous documents. This is not an intent to import an issue into an examination artificially. It arises naturally. I don't believe there's any question about the authenticity of this document. The issue of what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do you have any observation, Mr. Karadzic, on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Frankly, Mr. President, we also think it should be admitted, but we would like to have the same rules applied to many of the documents that we've offered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. It's clearly related to the document we admitted before, and as such, in particular given the accused's position, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1094, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, we looked a moment ago at the government session of the 10th of June, 1992, at which the conclusion that the Ministry of Justice should make a report about prisoners was made. If we could turn next to the government session of the 15th of June, 1992. That's 65 ter 00176. And if we could turn, with the assistance of the Registry, to page 4 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S. And it would be item number 10. That indicates as follows: "The government has considered the proposed report. It has been concluded that the issue of prisoners exchange is extremely important, complex and delicate, and that, if sufficient attention is not paid to it, it can cause a number of negative consequences for the whole republic. "It has been agreed that working group consisting of Professor Branko Djeric, Milan Trbojevic, Dr. Dragan Kalinic, Mico Stanisic, Bogdan Subotic, and Momcilo Mandic should consider all the aspects of the prisoner exchange problem and that they should proposal systematic and other solutions, taking into account our and international regulations. It is obvious that solving this problem is urgent and that the regulations and concrete measures for solving of this issue should be proposed as soon as possible." Now, first of all, Mr. Mandic, just to clarify for the benefit of the Court the persons mentioned in item number 10, we already know who Mr. Djeric is. Milan Trbojevic was the vice-president of the government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Kalinic was minister of health and social welfare, Mico Stanisic was the minister of the interior, Bogdan Subotic was the minister of defence, and I was the minister of justice. If I can be of assistance, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mandic. What?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have given you all the offices held by the members of this commission: Branko Djeric, the prime minister; Trbojevic, vice premier, in charge of internal policy; Kalinic, minister of health and social welfare; Mico Stanisic, minister of the interior; Bogdan Subotic, minister of defence; and I, minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And during the course of your testimony in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case, you were asked about this particular government session and this particular conclusion in the government session. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can help me, Mr. Tieger, to recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, after -- this is on page 9494, after that agenda item number 10 was read out. You were asked the following: "I know you weren't there, Mr. Mandic, but I assume Mr. Lale reported to you," Mr. Lale being a representative of the Ministry of Justice. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lale was the assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So just to continue: "I know you weren't there, Mr. Mandic, but I assume Mr. Lale reported to you. What was it that caused negative consequences?" And your answer was: "Since we were receiving bad news about ill-treatment of detained people in individual municipalities, the government decided to set up a very strong group consisting of the Prime Minister Djeric, Milan Trbojevic, Dragan Kalinic, health minister, Mico Stanisic, chief of police, Bogdan Subotic, defence minister, and myself, as the minister of justice, in order to consider all these problems and find quick solutions. That was a major problem for Republika Srpska and also for the people who were held in municipal detention units and prisons. That had to be given immediate attention and solved, and since this commission was not able to solve this issue, we had to include and involve the highest officials in order to prevent any unlawful arrests and detention of civilians."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not participate in the work of this commission, but I do know its objective, and it included health issues, defence issues, justice issues in its mandate, its basic task was to establish legal regulations for the work of the Central Commission and for the treatment of detained persons of non-Serb ethnicity. I explained a while ago that this was not done at government level, which I also confirmed when I testified in the Stanisic case, but I did mention that since the political leadership of Republika Srpska had been informed about it, Mr. Karadzic, the president of Republika Srpska, issued an order and instructed the minister of defence to issue, on his part, instructions on the treatment of detained persons of non-Serb ethnicity. In that way, the status of such persons, of detained persons or of prisoners of non-Serb ethnicity, was legally regulated and the way they should be treated. The regulations spelled out the treatment of such persons in full compliance with the 1949 Geneva Conventions on Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have -- I have a translation issue. The witness said "captured persons," persons taken prisoners. I don't think that is reflected. It should be "captured." It should not be "detained." That is not a proper translation. What he meant was "taken prisoner in battle," so can we have that clarified?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think that's purely a matter of interpretation. "In that way, the status of such a person, of detained persons or prisoners" -- I think that's a subject you can explore further during the course of your cross-examination. Let's proceed, Mr. Tieger. In the meantime, do you confirm that you said so during the course of the Stanisic/Zupljanin trial, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I confirm what is in the transcript, that that is what I said in the Stanisic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In that answer, you said, I quote: "We were receiving bad news about detained people in the municipalities." Could you expand on that a bit further? What kind of bad news were you hearing, and from whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received all our information from the prime minister, Mr. Djeric. Now, whether Mr. Djeric received information at the Presidency or in some other way, that I don't know. However, the disturbing news was that local authorities were not treating captured non-Serbs in the spirit of the Geneva Conventions and that they were violating human rights. The central government, that is to say, the Government of Republika Srpska and the Presidency, through these regulations and legislation, were trying to centralise matters, that is to say, to take over, to take over care and authority in the municipalities, in the regions, and in the centre, as it were. Perhaps I got a bit confused while explaining this, but we were trying to centralise authority, and we wanted these persons who had been taken prisoner to be treated in the spirit of the Geneva Conventions and human rights. That is why commissions were established. That is why an order was issued by the president of Republika Srpska. That is why instructions with the force of law were promulgated in the "Official Gazette," stating exactly how non-Serbs who were taken prisoner should be treated. That is what I meant, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I believe you indicated that notwithstanding the emphasis on the importance and urgency of this problem as raised in agenda item number 10, you did not participate in the commission.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I was probably busy with other urgent matters, because we were creating the judiciary. And this commission -- well, how the commission carried this through -- or perhaps I was out somewhere in the field, setting up prosecutors' offices and courts. Now, whether somebody was standing in for me or not, I really cannot recall. It's been a long time, and I cannot remember that particular detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to recap, before moving on to the next document: So on June 10th, the government called for a report. On June 15th, it received the report. The report indicated that the problem of prisoners exchange was extremely important and so on, and a working group was formed, or at least there was an agreement that a working group should consider all the aspects of prisoner exchange; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, Mr. Tieger. People worked day in and day out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's jump ahead one month to 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P1095.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's move forward now to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 01587, Mr. Mandic, is entitled "Report on some aspects of the work done to date and the tasks ahead," dated 17 July 1992, and coming from the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Ministry of the Interior. And it is -- the handwritten notation on the top -- on the cover page indicates: "To president of the Presidency and prime minister." Now, Mr. Mandic, you had a chance to see this document previously during the course of your testimony during the Krajisnik case?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably in one of these courtrooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, just to refresh your memory, let's look at a couple of the excerpts from that document. And you're more than welcome to take your time and look at the entirety of the document, if you need to. First of all, Mr. Mandic, let me direct your attention to the top of page 3 of the English, and in the B/C/S, page 4, also at the top of the page. And the report indicates as follows: "The army, crisis staffs and war presidencies have requested that the army round up or capture as many Muslim civilians as possible, and they leave such undefined camps to internal affairs organs. The conditions in some of these camps are poor; there is no food, individuals sometimes do not observe international norms, et cetera." Now, Mr. Mandic, did this document reflect generally the kind of information which was available to the government about what was happening in the field in connection with the detention of non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is dated the 17th of July, and it was submitted to the prime minister and the president of the Presidency or, rather, to the Presidency. Now, whether the government discussed this document, that is something I cannot recall. You probably have the minutes, and we can see whether it was discussed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, as I did in the course of the Krajisnik case, I attempted to ask you here not about a report specifically about this document, but about the information contained in the document. And as I asked in the Krajisnik case at 8944, directing your attention to this specific document and to this specific paragraph: "Mr. Mandic, you spoke earlier about irregularities and inhumane treatment in camp. Does this document, sent by the Ministry of Interior to the president of the Presidency and the prime minister on July 17th reflect generally the kind of information available to the government to which you were referring earlier?" And your answer was: "Yes." That's correct, isn't it, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall what I testified to six years ago. However, at this moment I cannot remember whether the government discussed this information. Obviously, concerning all information that reached the government and that the government discussed, the government would take measures in relation to such information and reports of the Ministry of Justice, of the Ministry of Police. I believe that this report is correct as well and that it reflects the situation on the ground. So there was concern on the part of the minister of police and the government that human rights were being violated in certain municipalities and in certain places where people acted unlawfully and against the Geneva Conventions and held prisoners. There is no reason for me to doubt this report of the Ministry of the Police. After all, it was compiled in order to overcome such situations and in order to establish rule of law, as I often say, and observe human rights, because all the documents until then had not provided for a situation when there would be war and when non-Serbs would be taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to a portion of the document approximately four paragraphs below that one, and that will be at page 4 of the B/C/S again and again on page 3 of the English. That indicates as follows: "It should also be noted that new territories are being liberated in combat activity and that even some Serbs are committing crimes, mainly all types of looting, in addition to the crimes previously committed by the enemy." And then it goes on to describe: "Looting, as the most serious crime against property, mostly occurs during mopping-up operations, on which occasions paramilitary formations, military formations and police engage in looting." And you were asked again about this document, and that particular provision was brought to your attention in the Krajisnik case, and you were asked in what manner were the new territories being liberated at the time the document was prepared and disseminated in the middle of July 1992. Do you recall that, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't recall such details. However, you can help me, can't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly. This is at page 8945: "Let me ask you this, then: What was the -- let me ask you: In what manners were new territories being liberated, if you know, at the time this document was being prepared in the middle of July 1992?" And you said: "As far as I knew, these were combat operations carried on by the army, police, and these crisis staffs. I was not very much familiar with that. I suppose these were combat operations and ethnic cleansing of the non-Serb population in some areas." And that was your testimony about that particular provision in the document; correct, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tieger, you say that I said "I assume." That means that I was not familiar with these combat activities. I could assume what was going on in the armed conflict; ethnic cleansing, combat. I was not a participant. I was not directly informed about that. This is basically an assumption, which is what I said when I testified in the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's turn to another portion of the document that you also commented on, Mr. Mandic, and that can be found at page 6 of the English and page 11 of the B/C/S. This paragraph found -- it's the last full paragraph at page 6 of the English, and I believe it's the last paragraph of the document in B/C/S as well, Mr. Mandic. And moving down to the last sentence of that paragraph, it states: "Special emphasis should be placed on the issue of relocating certain citizens, villages, et cetera, because this does not fall within the competence of the MUP, although efforts are being made to link it to the MUP." And, again, you were asked about that provision, Mr. Mandic. I take it it would be of some assistance for me to direct your attention to those portions.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you keep putting documents to me about which I presented my opinion and views in the Krajisnik trial. I accepted and confirmed that I still stand by everything I had said. That is to say, I confirm all the words I uttered by way of testimony in the Krajisnik trial. And now you're confusing me. You take out a few words or sentences, out of 12 typewritten pages, and you take them out of context, and I'm supposed to interpret that; problems between the police and the military. And at that time, I was head of the Civilian Sector of the Ministry of Justice, that is to say, a ministry that has nothing to do whatsoever with the military or with the police, especially not in relation to war operations. My effort to help the Court or you, Mr. Tieger, bring me in a position of confusion. You keep showing me these sentences and words that are extracted out of a larger context, and now I'm supposed to interpret them. I testified in Krajisnik six years ago in 2004, and I accept fully everything that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, do you see that paragraph before you, starting with: "With a view to resolving existing problems ..."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see that, Your Honour. It's the last one down there in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That concerns the functions of the Justice Ministry, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there was a military judiciary and a civilian judiciary. These problems fall under the military judiciary. So there was dual -- a dual judiciary, and I was head of the civilian judiciary. At that time, there was a military Ministry of Justice as well, that is to say, military prosecutors offices and prosecution organs. Obviously, these are problems between the military and the police, and there is an overlapping of powers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think I understand your statement. So the Ministry of Justice -- "Justice Ministry" in this paragraph refers to an organ in the army; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there was a military judiciary and a civilian judiciary. These are two completely separate judiciaries. I was head of the civilian judiciary, and I carried out the organisation of the civilian judiciary; courts, misdemeanor courts, prosecution offices, and institutions of correction, and they pertained to civilians only, or civilian institutions, rather. At the same time, there were military judiciary organs that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I understand there should be a military judiciary, but is there a separate ministry for military judiciary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, within the Ministry of Defence. It would be that ministry. They are a separate organ that has no points in common with the civilian judiciary. They have their own prosecutors, their own misdemeanor judges, and their own judges attached to the Main Staff, and the Main Staff of the army is the superior organ that organised the military judiciary. You will see, Your Honours, that several times I tried to bring that together and to create a single judiciary during the course of 1992. I think it was July and August 1992 when I asked that the Assembly amend the law and that there be a single judiciary. However, that did not happen while I was minister.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe that again it would be of assistance if the entire paragraph would be read out and if the witness would see the entire paragraph in Serbian. There is just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's what I suggested. We can continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, in response to my questions about the information contained in the document, you, among other things, indicated that your ministry had nothing to do with the military or the police. It's true, isn't it, that -- however, that you met quite often --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Problems between the army and police, problems and misunderstanding, operative ones, between the army and the police. That is what Mr. Stanisic said here, as far as I understand this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm less interested --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inter alia, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm less interested at the moment in the tensions between the military police than I am in the kinds of issues and crimes that are raised by the document. So let me ask you: It's correct, isn't it, that you met quite often with Mr. Stanisic, the minister of the interior, and of course this is a Ministry of Interior document, during which you discussed all these issues, including the criminality -- the crimes that were on the increase in the war-struck areas? And that can be found, in fact, at page 8951 of your Krajisnik testimony.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I met Stanisic as often as necessary, and that was basically at government sessions. The man was minister of police, and they were involved in armed operations together with the military, the army, and I was creating the judiciary. At my -- at the time of my appointment, there was no Ministry of Justice. At that point in time, Republika Srpska did not have a single judge, a single prosecutor, a single corrections institution. There was nothing that a ministry of justice could have in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mandic, again, I'm not asking you about what you may or may not have been in a position to do about it. I'm simply referring to your previous testimony that you met with Mr. Stanisic and that was one of the sources from which you were aware of these types of problems. And that's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it not correct that you met with Mr. Stanisic or not correct that you spoke about the problems of crimes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, several times you cut off in the middle of Mr. Tieger's questioning. Please hear him out and then start answering after you heard his answer [sic], please. Now, can you answer the question, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not remember what I discussed with Stanisic and whether we dealt with these topics, that is to say, problems on the ground in relations between the army and the police or, rather, the commission of crimes at the front-line. I'm explaining this for the purposes of the Court. All crimes that were committed in combat operations, in relation to the war, belonged to the military judiciary. All military conscripts from age 16 to 50 or 60 - I cannot remember the exact provision of the Law on National Defence - fall under military courts when there is an imminent threat of war, and that was declared in mid-April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I move on to the next question, I'm sure it will intrude into the time beyond which the Court indicated earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to tender this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson or Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Although the witness is not aware of the content of this document or the existence of it, it was read out during the course of the Krajisnik trial, and so he confirmed the situation in general. So, as such, it can be admitted as an inseparable and an indispensable part of the associated exhibit. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1096, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break, and we'll resume at --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are counting on reciprocity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to Mr. Tieger for having interrupted him. Please do accept my apology. I was just making an effort to say what I was thinking, so that my thoughts do not escape, as it were. So I do apologise, once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let's move on to another document shortly after the date of the document we just looked at, which was 17 July 1992, and this document is dated 20 July 1992. It's 65 ter 05531. Mr. Mandic, as you now see on the screen before you, this a document from the Security Services Centre, Banja Luka, to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP, for the minister. And although you can't see on this page, it's signed by the head of the centre, Stojan Zupljanin. Looking at the first paragraph, it indicates that: "During the months of April, May, June and July of 1992, in the wider area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, there were armed conflicts between the forces of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Muslim-Croat forces. We informed you about the progress and the results of those conflicts on a regular basis." And then if we can turn to the second paragraph, it refers to the arrest of a great number of citizens of Muslim and Croat nationality who were, depending on the number and the circumstances in the field, sent to various buildings, like schools, centres, factory facilities, open spaces and so on. The document then goes on to describe categories, and if you look at the bottom of the English on page 3, and I believe that's just at the top of page 2 of the B/C/S, it indicates that: "The third category is composed of adult men, about whom the service does not have any information of security for us so far. Therefore, they can be treated as hostages." Now, Mr. Mandic, you had the opportunity to see this document during the course of your testimony in the Krajisnik case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall this document, Mr. Tieger. I think that I see it for the first time right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, beginning at page 8956 of your testimony, this document was displayed as follows: "Can we turn next to a document dated July 20th, 1992, from the Security Service Centre of Banja Luka and directed to the MUP of Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for the minister." And your attention was thereafter directed to, initially, the first paragraph, which states: "We have informed you about the progress and the results of those conflicts on a regular basis," and then to the second paragraph, including the reference that I just read to you about the third category: "While the third category is made of adult men, about which the Security Service Centre does not have information of a security interest so that they can be treated as hostages." And, Mr. Mandic, I asked you at that time about a comment you had made earlier in your testimony, which was that -- and now I'm referring to page 8958 of the transcript, that you had said earlier in your Krajisnik testimony that: "The entire government, led by Mr. Djeric, requested that people not be detained, that civilians not be detained or deprived of liberty who had been incorporated into the war?" And you said: "Yes, that's correct." Now, that's with respect to Mr. Djeric's request that civilians not be detained?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the government's position, with Mr. Djeric at the helm, and I confirm that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then I asked you: "With respect to this document, Mr. Mandic, and was he referring to the civilians who are -- non-Serb civilians who are indicated in Mr. Zupljanin's letter of July 20th and in the previous report we saw from the Ministry of the Interior on the 17th of July?" And you said: "Yes, I think that's the case, yes." That was your testimony in the Krajisnik case, Mr. Mandic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by this. I confirm all my assertions which I made in testifying in the Krajisnik case. Is it necessary for me to repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I just wanted to bring this document to the Court's attention and tender the document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It was tendered originally as an associated exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- and during the course of the Krajisnik trial it was read out, and the witness confirmed it at the time. As such, it forms an indispensable or inseparable document from the transcript we admitted, so, as such, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1097, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, the situation described in both of those documents refer to a period a month or longer after the formation of the working group at the government session on the 15th of June. Do you know what steps, if any, the working group took to resolve the kinds of problems that are described in the two documents we've just looked at; that is, the July 17th, 1992, document and the July 20th, 1992, document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, this commission, i.e., working group, was formed on the 15th of July, and the reports are from the 17th and the 20th, so they were made after the setting up of the working group. I cannot recall whether they took any steps and, if so, what steps were taken, but obviously these reports were received a couple of days after the group had been set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Mr. Mandic, the working group, according to the minutes of the session of the government that we looked at, was set up on the 15th of June, not the 15th of July. Would you like to check the document again?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- yes, I believe you. It is okay. I do not remember that anything had been undertaken or in what scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, can we turn next to 65 ter 00184. That's a session of the government on the 4th of July, 1992. And if I can direct your attention to agenda item number 8, found on page 4 of the English, and I believe you'll find it at the bottom of page 4 in the B/C/S as well. That the provides as follows: "The question has been raised whether there are agreed criteria regarding the moving out of the Muslims population from the territory of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "It has been concluded that the government has not until now had a point of view on this matter. The Ministry of the Interior is entrusted with preparing information on this issue that the government would consider and take the appropriate standpoint." Now, first of all, Mr. Mandic, this was one of the reactions by the government to information of the type that was coming in to the government, and as we've seen in the documents we've just looked at; that is, information about the detention of non-Serb civilians and their treatment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I, myself, did not attend this government session, and obviously it was held before the 17th and 20th of July reports, so that I'm unable to state an opinion on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mandic, I wasn't suggesting that this was a reaction to those reports, specifically, but to the kind of information that was -- that existed and the kind of circumstances that prevailed around that time. So by the 10th of June, as you've indicated, the government was aware of the problem, and in the middle of June we've seen two reports indicating that the problem persisted. So I'm asking you now, as I asked you during the course of the Krajisnik case, whether the conclusion made by the government on 4 July 1992 was one of the reactions by the government to information of that type.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to repeat that I, myself, was not at that government session, that I'm unable to say anything on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's the passage of time, Mr. Mandic. Let me direct your attention to page 8959 and 8960 of your Krajisnik testimony. And on page 8959, you were presented with this document, that is, the minutes of the session of the government conducted on July 4, 1992, and you were asked about agenda item number 8 as follows: "Can I ask you to turn, Mr. Mandic, to agenda item number 8, that is, the last agenda item of the session, and it states as follows ..." And then the provision that we just looked at was read out. And then the question continued: "First of all, Mr. Mandic, was this one of the responses by the government or reactions by the government to information of the type we've just been looking at, reflected in the July 20th, 1992, document, or the July 17th, 1992, document?" And your answer was: "Yes, it was."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything now. Really, I was not at that session. I cannot adopt any stance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, with respect to the -- with respect to the criteria for Muslims moving out, what discussions took place about what acceptable criteria were for moving out Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know anything about that topic, Mr. Tieger. In fact, I do not know that that topic was discussed at all, as such. What moving out of Muslims are we talking about? I'm unfamiliar with the topic, as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you testified repeatedly during the course of the Krajisnik case about the detention of non-Serb civilians, their treatment in various detention facilities, the fact that that arose out of either collecting people from war zones or ethnic cleansing, and the government's -- and the government's expressed dissatisfaction with that situation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, in my testimony in the Krajisnik case, I merely talk about the penal/correctional facility in Butmir at Ilidza, where there was a lower court and a senior court on the premises of which I often was, and that is what I talked about and was familiar with. And I also talk about the positions and the conclusions of the government that I had contributed to. I believe that I have confirmed this in my past testimony, including that of today. On the other hand, I certainly do not know what happened in the autonomous province of Krajina, nor was I familiar with any element of the detention or, as you put it, moving out of Muslims. I really do not know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you suggested that the Ministry of Justice was not consulted in connection with the criteria for moving out of Muslims. Can you tell us why the Ministry of the Interior was tasked with responsibility in connection with the creation of appropriate criteria for moving Muslims out?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer to that question. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn next, then, to another July -- and I tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, given his answer in transcript page 8959 in the Krajisnik trial, I'm of the opinion that it also forms -- it forms an inseparable and indispensable part of that transcript. So, as such, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1098, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. President, I think a transcription problem with the numbers, but I think we'd like to turn next to 65 ter 40077.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, what I'm going to turn your attention to, as soon as it comes up on the screen, is a transcript of a television interview with Mrs. Plavsic in July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Could we see the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There's no date on the document, Your Honour. It was contextually dated in the Krajisnik case, and that's the -- it continues to be the basis for the date of the document, which is why I indicated by month rather than specific date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, as you can see here, and I'll give you an opportunity to cast an eye on that document, although I believe you had an opportunity to see that during the course of your Krajisnik testimony as well, Mrs. Plavsic is directing her attention to allegations about concentration camps, maintained by Bosnian Serb authorities, holding non-Serbs. And in the course of her interview, she's providing information about facilities that she indicates she was informed exist. And if you see in the middle of the first page in English, and that's also approximately the same place you'll find it in the B/C/S version, you'll see that she asked the official organs of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to comment on the list that was provided from Muslim authorities via UNPROFOR. And then if I can turn your attention to the bottom of page English -- the page 1 in English and in the middle of the first paragraph on page 2 in B/C/S, Mrs. Plavsic indicates as follows: "Here in Prijedor, there are actually 3.000 prisoners, and the location is Omarska. And those in detention are people who were sentenced by a judge, in accordance with the law and by regular procedure, to detention for a certain period of time." And then she goes on to talk about how those persons are categorised into -- and divided into three categories. Mr. Mandic, with respect to Mrs. Plavsic's assertion that the prisoners or detainees in the Omarska Camp were persons who were sentenced by a judge, in accordance with the law and by regular procedure, was that possible or impossible at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I should like to inform you that Biljana Plavsic was in charge of resolving the problems of detained non-Serbs on behalf of the Presidency of the Republika Srpska. One of her basic tasks was actually in that domain. Secondly, as far as I know, Omarska was a military prison, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I'll ask you again. Mr. Mandic, is it possible or impossible that the judiciary could have brought that number of people to Omarska through its procedures?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Omarska was a military prison, and if anyone was sent there, they were sent there by the military judiciary. It seems impossible to me that under the circumstances which obtained, such a large number of people were convicted and sent there. Actually, I have no comment on this. That will have to be seen with Mrs. Plavsic. As regards the civilian judiciary, it was in the offing, it was nascent in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, a couple of things, first of all, Mr. Mandic. First of all, if you look at the document, Mrs. Plavsic asserts that these were not concentration camps, and again I'm looking at page 1 of the English and, again, page 1 of the B/C/S, approximately the middle of the paragraph: "These were not concentration camps at all, but regular prisons, and it is completely normal that prisons exist in peacetime, but especially in wartime." And then she goes on to provide information that she says she received from the MUP, not from the military authorities. So I'm interested, first of all, Mr. Mandic, in how you know that Omarska was a military prison. When were you advised of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall. Probably after the war or perhaps during these events. I cannot remember when I learned. But I did hear that Omarska was a military prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So when Mrs. Plavsic refers to it as a regular prison in which there are judicial procedures, she was wrong; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing to say there. Of course she wasn't right. In Omarska, I don't think there's even a municipality. I don't even know what this place looks like, whether there's a court or prison or whatever. In the area of Omarska, a correctional facility was never established, even after I was minister. Obviously, Mrs. Plavsic is not really very well versed in the judiciary. You know, she got a doctorate in the field of snails. You know what snails are. She's a doctor of biology. She has no idea whatsoever about any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: She wasn't speaking as an expert in the field of snails, however, Mr. Mandic, was she? She was speaking as a member of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of -- of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how can she say that in such a short period of time, 8.000 persons can be prosecuted, tried, and sentenced? That is impossible. No one can say that, regardless of professional background. Obviously, she was saying it, I don't know, on the basis of propaganda or for the purposes of saying that to the public. It was the Muslim side that was accusing the Serb side, and then she was sort of wondering what that was all about and trying to give a professional explanation with regard to that, and we see how professional she is. I mean, you are an eminent lawyer, Mr. Tieger. You know how many trial chambers, prosecutors, judges, et cetera, you need in order to try 8.000 persons. I cannot say that this is sheer foolishness, but it's something along those lines. I really have no comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, again I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think we're going to be objecting to this one. Under your guide-lines, you've indicated when the parties are confronting a witness with the statement of another witness, then unless the witness adopts the content, it has to be introduced through, as you've termed, Witness A, the person who made the statement. And we feel this is an instance in which it is not admissible and it should be tendered through Mrs. Plavsic, who's also on the Prosecution's witness list. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, what did he say when asked about this during the course of the Krajisnik trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic indicated that it was impossible that the judiciary could have brought such a large number of people to Omarska through its procedures. If I may also add, this is not a statement in the sense that was raised with respect to the guide-lines. It's not a statement prepared for the course of this litigation. It's a contemporaneous statement by a member of the Presidency of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give us the page number in the Krajisnik trial transcript, Mr. Mandic's answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 9129, Your Honour.
