utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 9129. And -- sorry, Your Honour, and it was admitted as an exhibit during the course of Mr. Mandic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I know it is a part of the documents tendered as associated exhibits in relation to this transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Separate from the issue of how much weight should be given to this document, it forms an inseparable and indispensable part of Mr. Mandic's previous transcript. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1099, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mandic, with respect to Omarska, were you aware that the Omarska Camp was the focus of international attention after the international media gained access to the camp on approximately the 5th of August, 1992? First of all, do you recall the international outcry that resulted from the newspaper accounts and videos that emerged from that visit?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And does that mean that, in addition, at no time do you recall Omarska, in particular, being the focus of either attention by the international community or concern by the Bosnian Serb authorities about the international awareness of Omarska's existence and conditions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in any event, let me turn your attention, then, next to 65 ter 18413. Now, this document, 65 ter 18413, is a letter or some similar document dated 8 August 1992, directed to the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina president and to the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina prime minister. And I'll take you through the document, but I'll indicate that it's signed by the deputy minister for police affairs and tasks, Tomo Kovac. Now, Mr. Mandic, I've indicated earlier that the Omarska Camp and other facilities were the subject of international attention commencing August 5th. I understand that you have no recollection of that. But this document is dated 8 August, and if we look at the first paragraph, Mr. Kovac states in his document to the president and the prime minister as follows: "With the aim to resolve problems arising from the detention of other peoples - nations in certain facilities and collection centres in the zones of war activities, apart from the measures already taken by the government and its authorised ministries, I propose the following: that the status of these people be legally changed in compliance with international conventions on refugees, prisoners of war, et cetera." And continuing on to the second paragraph, Mr. Kovac refers to cases where MUP members accept or, in some cases, even take part in capturing people in the war zones. And after that, arrange accommodation and a way of life, and determine the duration of their attention and their entire destiny. And, finally, in that first page he refers to a much more important problem in the field is that people are not properly categorised in the facilities or collection centres: "We mean civilians and that category of prisoners of war who have committed criminal acts." And it goes on to discuss how those categories are to be treated. And, finally, I want to turn your attention to a couple of passages on the second page of the English, and that's exactly where you'll find them in the B/C/S as well. Mr. Kovac wrote to the president, the prime minister: "The civilian population, regardless of whether they belong to an ethnic group, extremist members of which are at war with the Serb Republic of BiH, may only have refugee status under the intensified control of the Serb MUP." And he goes on to discuss what sorts of conditions of life they should be provided, and then in the second-to-last paragraph states: "I am putting forward this problem in this manner because the international institutions will not recognise any other attitude towards members of other ethnic groups, regardless of the current situation our people are in, under the government of Muslim or Croat authorities." Now, Mr. Mandic, your attention was directed to this document during the course of the Krajisnik case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you did not dispute the circumstances that Mr. Kovac referred to, but you did dispute the sincerity of his letter in expressing concern about that; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I did not challenge or dispute or confirm what Mr. Kovac was saying. He was in charge of the uniformed police as assistant minister. What he wrote here on the 8th of August, as we've seen so far during my testimony, the government passed such conclusions several times. I think that this is an insincere letter written by Mr. Tomo Kovac. I cannot understand what it was that he wanted. I've already said this in the Krajisnik trial. He could not address the president of Republika Srpska and the prime minister directly. He had his own minister, his own deputy minister. He was supposed to resolve these problems within his own ministry. Now, why he did all this? This was mere repetition of these problems, and there were positions taken by his minister, too, so I don't know. I think this is simply insincere behaviour on his part. At that point in time, I do not know. I cannot use the term I would like to use, out of respect for the Judges and everyone else present here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mandic, in addition to the fact that this was directed to the president and prime minister directly, rather than via his own minister, it's also correct that you challenge the sincerity of this letter because this was the kind of information that the government had for a long time, and Mr. Kovac's belated expressions of concern appeared to you to be hypocritical; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, so far we have seen that the government on several occasions established a commission and expressed its concern over the information that was relayed by Mr. Djeric at government sessions. Certain measures were taken and commissions were established. Now, why does an assistant minister address the president of the republic and the prime minister directly in this way in relation to something that is already well known, in relation to which measures were already taken? And these local prisons, these illegal local prisons, were already being closed down. I think that during July and August, they had already been shut down on the basis of the order of the president of the republic, so I really cannot comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mandic, Mr. Kovac's letter was written on August 8th, immediately on the heels of the entry of the international media into the Omarska Camp. It wasn't shut down at that point. It wasn't shut down in July, was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I really don't know anything about Omarska. As far as I know, it was a military prison. When it was established, when it was closed down, I simply do not know. I do know, though, that in July and August, the government and the Presidency took a series of measures to shut down similar local prisons and military prisons that were not in the spirit of the Geneva Conventions and respect for human rights. You see, from April/May up until -- when the war broke out, until the 8th of July, it was only three months that had elapsed. You will see that many things -- many measures were taken by the Presidency, by the government, in order to prevent unlawful behaviour on the part of local staffs, paramilitaries, et cetera, and to regulate that area, in a way, because it had not been regulated up until the beginning of the war. Actually, war, itself, had not been envisaged or the detention of non-Serbs in the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mandic, in your answer you appeared to conflate the period July and August. So do I take it, by your earlier answer, that you are not aware that measures -- that any measures taken after the beginning of August were taken after an international outcry about the existence of detention facilities in which non-Serb civilians were held?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, Mr. Tieger, that Lord Paddy Ashdown, together with Dr. Karadzic, in the beginning of August visited the Butmir correctional facility in Sarajevo. I personally attended during that visit. As for other visits, and the outcry you are referring to, I know nothing about that, or, rather, I know very little. I was just informed to the extent to which Mr. Djeric spoke of these problems at government sessions. I believe that other institutions, military or any other, discussed military prisons and places where non-Serbs were kept by the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I want to -- we've discussed the Exchange Commission and the process of exchange to some extent. I'd like to turn now to some contemporary conversations that took place in the summer of 1992 and look at the extent to which they reflect the existence of the exchange process. Could we turn first to 65 ter 30847.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering that letter, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On the same basis, i.e., as an associated exhibit, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1100, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I don't know if you still have the binder of intercepts with you, but in this case I'm going to ask you to turn to the transcript of that particular conversation, because this is an intercept you've already listened to and authenticated during the course of your Krajisnik testimony. It's found at tab 18 of your binder, Mr. Mandic, and is a conversation between you and Mr. Krajisnik on the 26th of June, 1992. So I'll give you a moment to take a look at that and re-familiarise yourself with it.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mandic, the first page indicates the commencement of the conversation and some greetings exchanged. Turning to page 2 of the English, and I believe that's page 3 of the B/C/S, the numbers at the top of the page would be 0322-0983, Mr. Krajisnik asks, the passage that begins: "Yes, that has -- that is. Has he made it down there or not? It's all over now. Secondly, have you released the one I've told you about, by any chance?" "A. Yes, I have." That's your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "Yes? You, Mr. Mandic: "He left for Vrbanja one hour ago."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "Thanks God." You say: "Karamehmedovic; right?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "Yes, that's him." You say: "Well, he is gone." And we'll continue in a moment, but that's a reference to a Muslim who is released?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik asked me to find down there in Sarajevo, either in Butmir or in Lukavica, in one of the correctional facilities, a friend of his who was at that moment detained in Serb territory. In Lukavica, I found the man. I asked the military commander to release him, and I saw him off. Of course, I explained that this was a personal friend of the president of the Assembly. And I saw the man off to Vrbanja Most, where there was a line between Muslim and Serb-held territories, because I was there very often and I was there in the premises of the District Court in the Serb part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And during the course of the Krajisnik case, Mr. Menja [phoen] asked you if Karamehmedovic was somebody who had taken up arms against the Serbs or was suspected of being involved in criminal activity and, in general, why he was detained. And I believe you indicated you didn't know; you simply did what Mr. Krajisnik asked you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. I think that it was from the military authorities, from the commander of the corps down there, that I asked that the man be released. Now, how come this had happened in the first place, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, if we continue with this conversation, Mr. Krajisnik then asks you: "Let me also ask you what about this Savic, Milos, since it's his brother that is really ..." And then you say: "President, I put it on the list, the first next exchange and it will be finished." Now, Mr. Savic, this is a Serb who was detained by the Muslim authorities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Assembly, Mr. Krajisnik, informed me, as far as I can remember, that the brother of his secretary or the head of his office, Milos Savic, was arrested with his entire family in the Muslim part of Sarajevo, the federal part. Since I was down there in the District Court that was on the premises of the former correctional facility of Butmir, I insisted that the commission, the people who were working on exchanges, that they put on their list that entire family or another family, because he was very worried about his brother and his sister-in-law and two children, I think. That's what Mr. Krajisnik insisted upon. And I asked these people who worked down there -- I think it was some Eles [phoen] on behalf of the military and Vanovac [phoen] on behalf of Ilidza municipality. I can't remember now, but I know there was this inter-ethnic commission that made up these lists and that exchanges were carried out of persons who had been detained. I think that this Savic was exchanged for someone else who was held prisoner, and then he came to Serb-held territory. That was at the time when we were looking for a new president of the Central Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then, Mr. Mandic, as the conversation continues, there's a more general discussion about exchange. So after you say, at the bottom of page 2 of the English, and then continuing on into page 3 of the English, and it's page 3 of the B/C/S as well, after you say: "President, I put it on the list, the first next exchange and it will be finished."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK SAYS
utterances.text: "Check it down there. Do you have anyone there? Can you contact someone?" I'll let the siren stop. This is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- first-Monday-of-the-month siren. I think we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then, Mr. Mandic, you say: "There is this Vukovic, a member of the youth organisation, a Serb who is criticising us because we er ... have 400 prisoners here, you know?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK SAYS
utterances.text: "Who is criticising?" And you say: "I've got 400." And Mr. Krajisnik says: "And who is criticising?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MANDIC
utterances.text: "This Vukovic, Filip, the member of this youth organisation, Serb. He says - clean it, but er ... for them they are ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "Filip Vukovic?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MANDIC
utterances.text: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "Communist?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MANDIC
utterances.text: "Yes, yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "What does he want?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MANDIC
utterances.text: "He is the president of that Exchange Commission."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "Their commission?" And then you, Mr. Mandic: "Yes." And Mr. Krajisnik says: "And what is it that he wants?" And you say: "War prisoners, no, they are ex for them. They are hardly interested in people, they are interested in ammunition and meat, and now we let those women and children go to Vrbanja, to go to their own people, he says that's ethnic cleansing what we do ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "He does."

utterances.speaker: MR. MANDIC
utterances.text: "... here ... when ... I will fucking ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "And where is he now?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MANDIC
utterances.text: "Somewhere there, I do not know."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "With them, isn't he?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MANDIC
utterances.text: "Yes:

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "That means he is theirs?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MANDIC
utterances.text: "Yes, yes, yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "God, traitors are all around." And then you continue. You say: "Yes, yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK SAYS
utterances.text: "Good, Momo, look, please do call him. I would like to help Savic, it's his brother in stake ..." And you say: "Fist exchange, I will take care of that." And, Mr. Mandic, this portion of the conversation is a reflection of the awareness of Mr. Krajisnik, and yourself, and the Bosnian Serb leadership generally, of the Exchange Commission and its work; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik did not know anything about the work of the Exchange Commission. It is obvious from this conversation that he doesn't know who Filip Vukovic was and what he did, whether the man remained in federal Sarajevo or had passed over to the Serbian side. He was actually the head of the Commission of the Federation of B and H, of the Muslim side. So Momo Krajisnik, the president of the Assembly, was not at all familiar with the work of any of the commissions for the exchange of war prisoners. I was in Sarajevo, and I tried -- I did my best, according to the instructions of the government, to find a new president to appoint as president of the Central Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War because Rajko Colovic has resigned and went to Vlasenica to be the president of either the regular court or to Han Pijesak as a judge of the Military Court there. I'm not quite sure which.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It wasn't necessary for to you explain to Mr. Krajisnik what the Exchange Commission was, was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Momo Krajisnik didn't know anything about the work of the commission, to the best of my knowledge and in my opinion. He did not know at all what the role of this Filip Vukovic was or where this person was, and that person was the president of the Commission for the Exchange of POWs. It is obvious from this text that he didn't know anything, but I did. I knew because the government had authorised me to find a future president of the commission following the resignation of Colovic. This was a governmental body. It answered to the government. And, Mr. Tieger, its task was to co-ordinate the work of all the local commissions, the municipal and the regional ones, and to centralise their work, their lists, the exchange process, to liaise with UNPROFOR and the international community, as such, as well as with the federation. When I refer to the federation, I mean the Muslim side. Those days, that is what I did. I did my best to finish that specific job, in addition to my regular duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn next to another conversation about exchange. This one is 65 ter 30849.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The previous intercept --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- to be admitted. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1101, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is dated July 1, 1992. It's found behind tab 18 of your binder, Mr. Mandic. It's a transcript of a --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 18th, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this is another conversation which you had an opportunity to hear earlier and authenticate, so I'm showing you the transcript rather than replaying the entirety of the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, did you find the portion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mandic, if you recall that conversation. Generally, I'll direct your attention to particular portion of it, but I don't want to rush you in looking at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall this conversation, Mr. Tieger. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can turn to the second page in English, and I believe that's the second page in B/C/S as well. There is an exchange of greetings towards the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC ASKS YOU
utterances.text: "What's up, Momo?" You say: "Well, not much. I've just been to a government session, and I'm here now." And, in fact, Mr. Mandic, you recall that there was a government session on the 1st of July, 1992, that you did attend?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that. It was really a long, long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the official minutes of that session will confirm that, but we'll move on. And then you say -- after Mr. Karadzic has asked you what's up, you say: "We're working on an exchange now. We're evacuating some Serbs from Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija." And Mr. Karadzic says: "Oh, that's very important." And you say: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "We'll immediately," and then in slashes "mobilise," un-slash, "those fit for combat and the rest of them ..." And you say: "Yes, yes, we're evacuating them."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "How many will there be?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MANDIC
utterances.text: "Well, I don't really know. We have many on the list. There are 300 people from Hadzici, Muslims, who have been kept here for seven days. No one's inquired about them, no one seems to care. I don't know what do."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Why don't ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MANDIC
utterances.text: "No one's interested in them, these Muslims ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Yeah."

utterances.speaker: MR. MANDIC
utterances.text: "So we'll try to exchange them for these, umm ... people from Hrasnica and ..." And then I'll go on to the remainder in just a moment -- remainder of that particular passage in just a moment. So is it correct, Mr. Mandic, that this conversation reflects Mr. Karadzic's awareness of the exchange process and the availability of the exchange process?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, Mr. Tieger, Mr. Karadzic called me at the time on account of a friend of his, a certain Tomic, to check whether we had managed to return him to Sarajevo. Namely, sometime before that Mr. Karadzic called me and asked me to find -- whether in the military prison or in the prison which was then administered by the police, to find this person whose name I believe was Tomic. He was a Croat by ethnicity. I tried, through the police and through the army, to find the whereabouts of this person, and through these various persons who dealt with POWs I did not manage to find him. And I was informing Mr. Karadzic of that and [indiscernible] of the problems which had been relayed to me by members of the Exchange Commission. I liaised with the civilian president of the Exchange Commission and the staff in charge of Ilidza and Mr. Ellis. They had informed me, inter alia, that somebody had come from Hadzici or perhaps the army had brought them there, these people, and these people wanted to go via Vrbanja to federal Sarajevo, but the Muslim side would not admit them because they had no accommodation, no food for them, and they didn't want them there. So that was the problem, the exchange problem that these people who worked on the exchange process had informed me about, and I was informing in this conversation Dr. Karadzic about it. I was also informing him about whole families of Serbs detained by the Muslim forces in a school in Hrasnica. And they proposed to me, if they didn't want to admit these people from Hadzici, to admit them to Sarajevo, that they be exchanged for these Serbs from Hrasnica. And this is what I was informing Mr. Karadzic about, and I was telling him what I knew specifically about these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what was it that Tomic had done to find himself in detention and subject to exchange?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I never found this person, I never established contact with him, nor do I have any idea what he might have done. I looked for him in the military prison and in this other prison, but I was unable to find him. I never found the man. To my knowledge, he had been released. Whether he lived on Dobrinja because of the war operations or what, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, carrying on with the conversation, there is a discussion about Tomic, and you say: "President, he's definitely not there. All Croats are gone. There are no more Croats in Kula." And then you go on shortly thereafter to say: "President, all Croats have been exchanged. Here, let me check again. I'll call you back in five minutes." So at that time, there was an awareness of who was detained by ethnicity, so that you were in a position to say that all Croats had been exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I asked the representatives of the police and the army to find whether they had a person by the surname of Tomic. I didn't know his name. President Karadzic had told me that this was a Croat and a friend of his. So I asked these people again, these people who had these exchange lists. On the list, there was no Tomic, so that means that he just wasn't there. So I inquired, through the police and the army and members of the Exchange Commission, I inquired about this person, and I never found him. And I did that because I was assigned this task by the president of the republic; namely, to find this friend of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1102.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I'd like to take a look at what was happening at the time, as reflected in other contemporaneous conversations. And perhaps we can take that chronologically, and we'll look at approximately three conversations. The first is from the 5th of May, 1992. That's found at tab 22 in your binder, and it's 65 ter 30734. Now, again, Mr. Mandic, this is a conversation you had an opportunity to hear and authenticate before. It's relatively long, so I don't want to play it in its entirety again and then refer you back to particular passages. So perhaps you can take a moment to re-familiarise yourself with it, and I'll direct your attention to particular portions.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this conversation, Mr. Tieger. You can ask me your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. So this is a conversation between you and Mr. Branko Kvesic and Mr. Bruno Stojic. And they were both former members of the joint MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The first portion I want to direct your attention to is found on page 4 of the English and the page marked "0109" in B/C/S, which is the fourth page or fifth page, I believe. I think you'll see the numbers at the top of that page, "0322-0109." And there it appears that you and Mr. Kvesic are talking about positions in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KVESIC ASKS
utterances.text: "So are right there in Pale, are you?" And you say: "Well, we are not. We came down to the city." And Mr. Kvesic says: "Yes, yes." You say: "We came down and cleaned Grbavica ..." Kvesic says: "Is that so?" And you say: "There, we hold Ilidza, Dobrinja and Nedzarici, all the way to student campus and so on." And is that -- Mr. Mandic, is that generally a description of at least some of the positions held by the Bosnian Serbs at the beginning of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, Mr. Tieger, I told Kvesic and Bruno Stojic -- we knew that Mr. Munir Alibabic was having this conversation recorded, it was being intercepted, so we mocked him in a specific Bosnian or, shall I say, Serbian way. We were trying to, yeah, joke about the advancing of the 182nd and the 3rd Armies. This was more like a jocular conversation of former associates, some of whom had gone to be with their people, the Croats, and others with their people, the Serbs. And I did everything on purpose. I exaggerated everything on purpose. I was ridiculing Munir Alibabic and his staff, who were listening in on our conversation and making these reports, because a couple of days before that they had aired some of our conversations on television and had spoken in very bad terms about some of my associates. So I believe that this was a flippant conversation on our part. It wasn't something reflecting the actual situation in the battle-field or something which was consistent with our actual mood at the time. This is what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I understand, Mr. Mandic, that your -- your assertion that you're attempting to tweak Mr. Alibabic. So when you refer to holding Ilidza, Dobrinja and Nedzarici, all the way to the student campus, is that generally accurate and is there, therefore, an attempt to rub his nose in that, or is that not accurate?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we knew that Mr. Munir Alibabic was having the conversation recorded. I knew it, and I told Branko so. At that moment, we were -- I mean, myself and Munir Alibabic were at opposite sides, on opposite sides, because all these intercepts that you have are by Munir Alibabic, who made them a year before the war, and during 1992 he was actually obsessed with me and recorded all my conversations and then combined them also. Why? Because in 1991, we had had a falling-out, a conflict, because he, as the chief of the Sarajevo State Security Centre, had started to record -- intercept everything that was Serbian in the police, in the political circles, and he would take those intercepts to the Party of Democratic Action, the president of which he was, who was president. He had locked up in the 1980s -- sorry, in the 1980s, and also convicted to eight years of prison. Now what he was doing, he was seeking to ingratiate himself, to curry favour with those very same persons and that very same person. You know, Mr. Tieger, how well he co-operated with you. He brought you just the recordings of one side, not of the other side, and he didn't bring you the recordings of the other side's conversations because he spoke in very foul language about me, my family, et cetera. At the end, at the proposal of your former boss, Mr. Tieger, Madam Carla Del Ponte, Munir Alibabic was prohibited to work in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the police, in police organs, until the end of his life. That kind of a person -- that kind of a man, who was my personal enemy or opponent or rival, a person who built his career on this kind of exercise, was the person I was up against, and in this way I was trying, actually, to mock his behaviour and to rub his nose in it, to tweak him, as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at some of the subjects that you chose to use to rub his nose in it. If we could turn to page 5 of the English, and that would be page 0110, at least as marked at the top of the page, in B/C/S. And there, Mr. Kvesic asks: "Yeah, what else is going on?" And you say: "Well, we're holding Turks under siege. We'll starve them a bit, you know." Kvesic: "Are you?" And then you say: "And then we'll give them everything from the Eternal Flame to Vratnik, everything up there." And then both you and Mr. Kvesic laugh. Mr. Mandic, the reference to holding the Turks under siege and starving them a bit is a reference to the encirclement of Sarajevo by the Bosnian Serb military authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the moment, I wasn't referring to that. I was not aware of that. I explained a bit ago I was trying to actually mock this person who was recording us and then would rush that recording to Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So maybe I didn't understand you perfectly, Mr. Mandic. Does that -- you said you weren't aware of that. Does that mean that you just made up the concept of holding Turks under siege out of old cloth and had no previous awareness of it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I was aware, I had an idea, but the Muslim public insisted on it, on the encirclement of Sarajevo, on everything else, and they insisted that the Serbs had fled to the woods up there; that these were forest people, wood people, as they called them. So we chose another way to mock them. We said that they were the army of the federation that had reached the Eternal Flame, the Eternal Flame being the center of Sarajevo. You are too serious a man, Mr. Tieger, to understand the kind of haggling in the Sarajevo manner which is peculiar to just that city and to those people there, irrespective of their ethnicity, whether Serbs, Croats, or Muslims. Prior to the war, there was a show -- there was a programme, The Theatre of the No-Smoking Group, which divided Sarajevo. In the morning, they would smuggle goods; in the evening, they would fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll be continuing with this, but I know we're already slightly past the time and I don't want to impose on the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. We'll have a break for an hour, resuming at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, before we adjourned, we were looking at some of the passages from the 5 May 1992 conversation with you and Mr. Kvesic and Mr. Stojic. I just want to turn your attention to two or three more of those portions. If I could ask you to turn to page 7 of the English and to the page that is marked "0322-0112" in the B/C/S. And those portions are also depicted on screen at the moment. At this point, Mr. Stojic comes into the conversation, and the conversation begins: "Where have you been, my Serb brother?" You say: "Where have you been, my free Croat brother?" There's laughter. Then Mr. Stojic says: "What is this that you are doing, you mother-fucker?" And you say: "We want to build a new and nice Sarajevo." And Mr. Stojic says: "New and nice Sarajevo?" And you say: "Yes. We don't like this old synagogues and mosques. We have to change architecture and everything." Now, Mr. Mandic, I know you've explained that, in part, you were attempting to tweak or rub Mr. Alibabic's nose in this, but this reference to changing the architecture and building a new and nice Sarajevo is a way to tweak him by referring to the shelling of Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was the 5th of May. That was a conflict between the Serb and Muslim police at Vrace. There was no shelling of Sarajevo then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what was the reference to changing the architecture of synagogues and mosques about, then?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there's only one synagogue in Sarajevo. It was a joke, Mr. Tieger. I don't know if you can appreciate that, as a serious lawyer, that kind of joking in the Sarajevo milieu, that is. On the 5th of May, there was no bombardment of Sarajevo. There was only a clash between the Serb special police and the reserve police force at Vrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was the bombardment anticipated at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question of yours. These are assumptions. I'm a witness here. I'm not an expert. Robert Dolip [phoen], in his findings in the Galic case, stated that on the 6th of April, the attack started -- or, rather, the shelling of Sarajevo started when the Police Academy was attacked. That is, the old nucleus of Sarajevo. Of course, that's not correct, because then, on the 6th of April, it was the Serb police that was at Vrace, and it wasn't on the 5th. If you remember, after the clash at Vrace at the School of the Interior -- the Ministry of the Interior, it was the Serb police that stayed there and there was no shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You referred earlier to mocking the Muslims about reaching the Eternal Flame, the Eternal Flame being the center of Sarajevo, I believe you said. And I want to turn next --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I want to turn next to a couple of references to that. First, on page 8 of the English, and in B/C/S, Mr. Mandic, that would be at the page marked "0322-0113." First, in that passage, this is a continuation of you and Mr. Stojic, and together the two of you, toward the top of the page in English, are laughing about Muslims having pushed you Serbs all the way to Skenderija. And then this passage: Stojic asks: "Listen, is there any way to resolve this peacefully?" And you say: "What?" And Stojic says: "Well, this in Sarajevo." And then you say: "Only when they give up everything from Skenderija and around there, then we will accept, and leave for them everything from the Eternal Flame all the way up." And Stojic says: "But they are left with nothing then." And you say: "Fuck them. They didn't want to do it nicely through negotiations. Well, now they'll get nothing." So is it correct, Mr. Mandic, that the earlier reference to the Eternal Flame, that is, leaving the Muslims to the Muslim Army at the Eternal Flame, the joke there is they are being pushed into a very small part of Sarajevo? In other words, is the tweaking that you're doing at this point, that the Muslims are doing badly, you're saying that the Bosnian Serbs will only accept leaving them everything from the Eternal Flame, and Stojic and you make clear that leaves the Muslims with very little?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused, once again, by your going back to this conversation. Mr. Tieger, I had explained in detail what kind of conversations I had with the Croats. Of course, we have to establish together that the Croats were also a warring party, and mainly against the Serbs. Bearing in mind that our conversation was being intercepted by Munir Alibabic in Sarajevo at the PTT, these were jokes. This was not serious. This was bragging so that the Muslims, Alibabic, would hear this; that Mujahedin units had reached Pale, Romanija, that Radovan Karadzic had fled to Switzerland, I can't remember which city there, with loads of valuables and so on. So if you take that out of context, it doesn't work, whereas the Eternal Flame is in Tito Street, as it was called at the time, in the center of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Last reference in this conversation, Mr. Mandic, this time to a portion of the conversation where Mr. Stanisic picks up the line and is speaking to Mr. Kvesic. And that's found at page 23 of the English, and in B/C/S at the page marked "0322-0129." And the reference I'm drawing your attention to, at the top of the page in English on 23, is Mr. Stanisic speaking, saying: "We are trying to drive them out without losses, but it seems that they don't want to go away." And Kvesic says: "Where? Where the hell do you want to drive them to? Up to Bascarsija, down to Pale? Where? They have no place to go." And then Mr. Stanisic laughs. Sorry, Mr. Mandic, I see you're still looking for it. If you look at the top of the page, you'll see that the ERN numbers that are marked, the first four numbers are usually 0322, and then the particular page is 0129. In any event, it's on the screen. Mr. Mandic, is that another joke based on the fact that the Muslims are being driven into smaller parts of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, according to Munir Alibabic, this conversation took place on the 5th of May. I don't know what Mico Stanisic knew about driving the Muslims into smaller parts of Sarajevo or not, or perhaps it was based on the same knowledge that I had spoken of a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. I started with a conversation in early May. Let me turn you a couple of months ahead to the beginning of July, and specifically July 10th. That's -- and, Your Honour, I would tender the previous document, 30734.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1103, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you're going to find this next document in tab 24 of your binder, and that's, again, a conversation of the 10th of July, 1992 with Mr. Mandic, Mr. Rezo, and then Mr. Mandic and Mr. Kvesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The 65 ter number, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 32672, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Mandic, looking at this, this is a conversation you had a chance to hear in its entirety and then authenticate in the Krajisnik case. Looking at it again today, do you recall it? And, again, it's relatively long, so if you need a moment or two to look at it, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just go ahead and put your question to me, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, let me ask you to turn to what is contained in page 7 of the English, and in the B/C/S that's found at the page marked "0328-2472." And here, on July 10th, you say to Mr. Kvesic, who asks: "Tell me when this is going to finish, to hell with it." You say: "I don't know. Believe me, I don't know. It probably depends on those three men. Actually, it depends on your boss and mine. I think that they could exert a lot of influence in order to get this finished as soon as possible." Kvesic says: "Yes." You say: "There is no sense to wage a war now, you know." Kvesic says: "No fucking way." You say: "Counties and national communities have already taken everything that was supposed to be taken. I don't know. Sarajevo is disputable, the area down there in Herzegovina and up there along the Sava River. There is nothing left." Mr. Mandic, is that portion of the conversation a reflection of the fact that by July, much of the area or territory sought by the Bosnian Serbs that was considered supposed to have been taken had already been taken?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could turn your attention, in that connection, to 65 ter 00028. That's a session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, the 17th session, held on July 24th through 26th, 1992, which I believe you attended, Mr. Mandic. And I would direct your attention to the English at page 18, and in B/C/S it's page 16. If we go one more page forward, please, in English. Thank you. This is Dr. Karadzic speaking, and he says on that date: "Militarily, we are in an excellent position. Our foreign political position is terrible. Our domestic political situation is very good, being that our people are fully in favour of fighting, that is, peace, because we don't have any more reason to fight. We have liberated almost everything that is ours. In final talks, we could even return some territories, villages that do not belong to us." And, Mr. Mandic, was that the position that you were reflecting when you were speaking with Mr. Kvesic in July, that -- or was it consistent with the position that you took, that everything that had been taken -- that was supposed to be taken had been taken, for the most part?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, if I could ask you to turn next to what appears on page 8 of the English, and the page marked "0328-2472" of the B/C/S. In the middle of the page in English, Kvesic is talking about some of the alternatives and organisation according to counties, and you stop him and say: "Wait a minute. But they are a minority now, man." He says: "What?" You say: "They are a minor now, fuck." And he says: "There's no way to build a military --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Are we following the -- you're referring to page 8 of that intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. I'm sorry, my apologies to the Registrar. I did not assist the Registrar in moving back and forth. So with that understood, can we move back, please, to 32672 and to page 8 of the English, and page 0328-2472 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, it is, again, the July 10th conversation at tab 24 of your binder, and --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The page number would be -- if you look up at the top, you should see it at 0328-2472. I believe it's the fifth page in sequence. And it is shown on screen. And, again, I was directing your attention to the portion where you say: "Wait a minute. But they are a minority now, man." Kvesic says: "What?" You say: "They are a minority now, fuck." Kvesic says: "There is no way to build a unitary country, either Serbian or Croatian, any more." And you say: "They are the smallest nation in number now." Mr. Mandic, we looked at a similar sentiment expressed by Mr. Kupresanin earlier in your examination. Is that a reflection of the awareness that -- of the demographic change that has occurred -- and I see you nodding -- the demographic change that has occurred and the reduction of the Muslim population in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tieger. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the territories that were held by the Bosnian Serbs. Obviously, at that point in time, the Bosnian Serbs held the larger part of Bosnia-Herzegovina under their control. That's what Mr. Karadzic said to the Assembly as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me just a moment. I'm just fixing the technical capacity here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mandic, if I could next direct your attention to page 11 of the English, and that would be at page 0328-2474 in the B/C/S. And I'm looking at the bottom of the page in English, and I think you'll find that in approximately the middle of the page in B/C/S. So Kvesic begins: "There are some of our men in Manjaca, man." And you say: "In Krajina, right?" And he says: "Yes." And you say: "We can do it." He says: "What can you do about it?" You say: "A lot." Kvesic says: "Listen, fuck, let's find out. Listen, it is because of relations in general." You say: "Naturally, man." Kvesic says: "There is ..." And then you say: "All right, I'll tell it to my main boss." And Kvesic says: "Check it, please." You say: "Where are they placed?" Kvesic says: "You know where I am?" You say: "I know it, but where are they placed over there?" He says: "They are placed somewhere in Manjaca." And you say: "Over there in the military camp in Manjaca?" And that's a reference to the Manjaca camp in the Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, first of all I'm asking whether this Manjaca is in Krajina, and then Kvesic confirms that for me, because I didn't know where this Manjaca was at all. Just read what I said in the Stanisic case. Try to remember what I said there. You take it out of context, and then it gets a completely different meaning. Branko Kvesic asked me about this Medjarevic [phoen], who was from the same area that he was from, and he claimed that he was in Manjaca as well. And I asked him, Is that in Krajina? I mean, I'm asking whether Manjaca is in Krajina. And he says to me, Yes. And then I tell him that through my main boss, I would see what could be done for that Croat. I did not know at all where Manjaca was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mandic, I did read your Stanisic/Zupljanin testimony. I think that position was challenged there as well. It's correct, and I don't want to quibble about this point unnecessarily, but Kvesic simply says, They're in Manjaca, and you say, In Krajina; right? So you're the one who raised the fact that it's in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking. You can see the question mark. I'm asking, Is it in Krajina, is it in Krajina at all? And I fully stand by my statement in the Stanisic case in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Mandic, in the interests of time, I want to move on to a somewhat different topic, and that is the issue of paramilitaries, if I may. And I think you discussed that to some extent also in your Stanisic/Zupljanin testimony. So let me first direct your attention to a quote from the 22nd Assembly -- Bosnian Serb Assembly held toward the end of November 1992. That's 65 ter 00035.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, we'll admit that intercept, 32673, as Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 32672 will be admitted as Exhibit P1104. And for the record, 65 ter number 28 has been already admitted as Defence Exhibit 92.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, let me just ask you a couple questions about the 22nd Assembly session, Mr. Mandic. That was the session at which there was considerable discussion involving Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Djeric, yourself, Mr. Stanisic, about the -- about a number of issues related to the government, including who you and Mr. Stanisic reported to, the extent to which there was conflict between you and Mr. Stanisic, on the one hand, and Mr. Djeric, on the other, and other issues; correct? And it's the session at which that current government of Mr. Djeric's fell? Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that session, Mr. Tieger. Please go ahead with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, during the course of your Stanisic/Zupljanin testimony, when you were asked about the relationship between Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Djeric at page 9724, you pointed to what you refer to as a clash between them on the issue of paramilitary formations. Do you recall that, generally? I'll direct your attention to the specific portion in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you said that Mr. Djeric followed Mrs. Plavsic and that she said at the Assembly -- or she explained at that particular Assembly session how she invited Arkan, and his Tigers, and the White Eagles, and what you referred to as other animals and beasts, into Republika Srpska? That's at 9724 through 9725.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Ms. Biljana Plavsic was an advocate of having all paramilitary units from territories where Serbs lived outside Bosnia and Herzegovina coming to the assistance of their brethren in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the religious war being waged there. Mico Stanisic, the chief of the police and the legalist, was against it, and I supported him, and Mr. Djeric supported Biljana Plavsic. At that session, she said, I have people called Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, his Tigers, the White Eagles, the Ducks, the Crows, et cetera, the Magpies, to come and fight on the Serbian side, and our minister of the police is arresting those people, which he did with the Yellow Wasps, and he's preventing our brethren coming to our assistance. That was the culmination of the clash between Biljana Plavsic and Mico Stanisic; i.e., Djeric and Biljana on the one hand and me and Mico Stanisic, on the other hand, because these para groups, in the territory where control was held by the Serbs, when they had nothing to loot anymore from the non-Serbs, they would then proceed to loot the Serbs, the property of the Serbs. That is what the minister of the interior tried to put an end to. He informed this government session about this, Mr. Djeric at government sessions, and he asked for Ms. Plavsic not to conduct such a policy. But professors being professors, they took it personally, and the conflict, in terms of how the state should be led, was transferred to the personal plane, to a personal conflict. So they looked for a reason to remove Ministers Mandic and Stanisic because their course was on a collision course with their own. The political party in power then respected the stance of Biljana Plavsic rather than -- after she had said at that government session -- at that Assembly session that she had invited explicitly paramilitary units to come to Bosnia and commit crimes, in my opinion, she should have been relieved from her office, and in that case and had that been done, there would be far fewer representatives of the former authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina sitting right here. That was the mistake. In my view, those who abided by the law, who created the law, who were legalists, should have been respected rather than those who pleaded the Serbian case, saying that out of 12 million Serbs, 6 million should perish in order for the other 6 million to live in liberty. So Mrs. Plavsic was not a nationalist. She was an evil person who said these things out of her own personal motives. She portrayed herself as the Serbian mother, but I, myself, and some other people know that she was actually a jilted woman. She had been jilted by her lover of Muslim nationality, and this was the way she was exacting revenge on everybody else, by the stances which she adopted in these assemblies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you also explain in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case, Mr. Mandic, that at that particular session Djeric singled you and Stanisic out, claiming that you had, and you in particular, had ties with Karadzic, and you pointed out how unfair that was, in your view, because: "I wouldn't exchange a word with Karadzic for half a year because he allowed Plavsic and others to do this." That is, to call in the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not at all close to Mr. Karadzic. Ours were only official contacts, and ours were only official conversations. From that time in early 1992, when some of the Serbian sycophants went and told to the president of the republic that it had been my idea and Alija Mustafic's idea that we should see to it that Radovan and Alija should cool down a bit and for tensions to ease some, that was an expression of mistrust in me, as a person, as a man who was prepared to do many things that others were not prepared to do. I had no privileges whatsoever in respect of the treatment accorded me by the president of the Republika Srpska. In fact, on several occasions, Biljana Plavsic and Professor Koljevic showered lies on Mr. Karadzic regarding my activities and actions and those of Mico Stanisic, and actually the late Dr. Koljevic admitted to that in the Villa Bosanka at a certain point in the past, and that was for the first time in my life that I heard Dr. Radovan Karadzic cursing God, swearing at God. It is a fallacious view, Mr. Tieger, that I had been in any way the favourite of Mr. Karadzic's. In fact, he had reservations -- unjustified reservations towards me, although I did my hardest to do everything honorably, decently, complying with the law, et cetera. You will see that the Ministry of Justice, over the period of a year or perhaps 10 months, was created, and it still functions to this very day upon those very foundations in the republic. I did have the support of Dr. Karadzic at that time, especially in the selection of non-Serb personnel, both in the prosecutorial and the judicature offices in general, but Mrs. Plavsic was against this. She was always saying that I was, you know, fishing in murky waters, or this and that, which was totally unfair in my regards. Mr. Tieger, I was practically driven away to Belgrade in that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just an intervention. Not only prosecutorial, but also support for the court organs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter believes she said "judicature."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [In English] Probably "judicial." [Interpretation] It should be "judicial." [In English] Prosecutorial and judicial. [Interpretation] Because the ministry proposed the prosecutors and the court staff, the judicial staff too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, thank you for that information, some of which you had alluded to earlier. But I had asked you about something you said in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case in connection with Plavsic's invitation to paramilitaries to come to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you had said the following at page 9726, referring to Mr. Djeric: "He singled out me and Stanisic, and he said I had ties with Karadzic, and yet I wouldn't exchange a word with Karadzic for half a year because he allowed Plavsic and others to do this." And that's a quote. That's what you said in Stanisic/Zupljanin; is that correct, Mr. Mandic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that what is in the record is quite correct. I was not angry with President Karadzic because I had been sent to Belgrade, because I had intended to go there in autumn 1992, in agreement with Djeric. And that was not much of a problem to me, personally, because my family was in Belgrade and I, in a way, wanted to go there. My son was a cadet at the Military Academy in Belgrade from 1991, and my other son and my wife were there. But the way in which, actually, conditions were placed on this by Biljana Plavsic, in contravention of the International Law and the legislation of Republika Srpska, the way in which she violated these was something that angered me and was the cause of my dissatisfaction. But she was a great authority there, in some segments even a greater authority than the president of Republika Srpska, and evidently now we can see what some of her positions have led to, totally without reason. The Serbs had a good army. We had a good organisation, we created a judiciary, the police force. We did not want not to live side by side with our Muslims. We were afraid of some new Muslims who were differently inclined, who wanted to introduce religious laws into state institutions, the Shiite laws, et cetera. Mr. Tieger, let me just finish my sentence. We were afraid of these new Muslims who were not turned towards Turkey and Ankara, which was a secular state, but would turn and look up to Iran, the religious states, and that could create problems for our state. You can see that now these self-same Muslims are blowing up police stations in their own federation, in the federation, because it is a state of the kind that it is. We didn't have any problem with our own Muslims, so to speak. We wanted to live together with them side by side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mandic, just so I'm clear and the Court is clear about your position about the paramilitaries that Mrs. Plavsic invited in: In the course of your Stanisic/Zupljanin testimony, you refer to them as people who torch, rob, kill, kill children, and is that an accurate reflection of your view about those paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you have again extracted my testimony, a part of it, from the context. I said that some of the paramilitary units, which came from other countries other than from Bosnia-Herzegovina, were criminals and did not want to subject themselves to the control of the army and the police, and it is true they did kill non-Serbs and loot their property. But once there were no more non-Serbs to kill or loot, they did the same to the Serb population. They killed Serbs, they looted their property, they raped their women. They were criminals, and those of their ilk were arrested by Mico Stanisic, to my knowledge. But Ms. Biljana Plavsic was opposed to all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to some contemporaneous conversations or documents related to the paramilitaries and see if they are consistent with your information or if you know something independently about them as well. The first one would be 65 ter 30712.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, have we looked at any paragraph in that 22nd session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't remember we looked at a specific paragraph in the minute, because the witness said he knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. We moved on pretty -- to some other issues. It's at pages 19 and 20 of both the English and the B/C/S, and it might be useful to look at an excerpt --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I've re-told it all to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could admit the first page, as we saw the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you're minded to tender that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The transcript or the minute of that 22nd Session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I had intend to do look at the particular excerpt. I think that -- I think we were in agreement that that session, along with the others, will be admitted over time. I'm more than happy to look at the particular portion of that session at which Mrs. -- during which Mrs. Plavsic is speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's up to you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, if the Assembly session is tendered, we can look at it at leisure. I don't think it's going to change the witness's mind about what was said, particularly, but I'm -- again, it won't take long to look at it, if the Court is minded to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it is objected to, that session transcript will be admitted as ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1105, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And at the end of today's session, if you could tell us where we are, in terms of your intention to tender those session transcripts or the like. We'll come to that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honour, I'll be happy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I had just been about to play for you and the Court 30712. We have to go to Sanction to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Good morning. It's Biljana Plavsic. Is Zeljko there?" "No, he's not up yet. Mr. Rus is here. Do you want to speak to him?" "All right, put him on." "Hello." "Good morning." "Good morning. My deepest respect, madam. How are you?" "I'm the commander's batman." "I know, I know." "Just getting ready for the raising of the flag." "Ah, the raising of the flag. I won't hold you very long." "No, no, no problem at all." "Let me ask you something. Zeljko is not there; right?" "Well, you know what? I would like to ask you if you wouldn't mind telling me, if you can, that is, when you would call again so that I can tell him." "You know why ... I'm ..." "Well, he's got to bed. He was in the field, and ..." "All right, all right, never mind. This is what it is about. I have returned to my base, the one where I am from." "Hold on ... all right." "Yes, but I haven't arrived home yet. One small part was blocked. But I wanted -- ask him if we asked him to come here, if that was possible in theory." "Look, ma'am ..." "So then I'll -- from whom -- I don't have the authorisation to speak on his behalf." "I know, of course." "But in any case, I'll give him your message immediately." "Yes, give him the message. When I get to my apartment, I'll ..." " ... call him." "Yes, and then I won't ask this. I'll just ask if you can possibly bring the merchandise." "Understood, understood." "Sure?" "Yes, bravo, very clever." "Right. Look, ma'am." "Yes." "If you can call him ... just let me check the time. It's 8.00 now. So if you can call him in about two hours, I'll tell him that --" "All right." "In an hour or ..." "All right, all right." "So you won't worry about that." "Right, give him my regards." "I'm really sorry that the situation is like this now ... he really is not up ... you know, he's always there from the raising of the flag, but he went -- for the raising of the flag, but he went to bed very late." "All right. Tell me, how are things in Zvornik?" "Sorry?" "How are things in Zvornik? Did Pejo go there?" "Well, I don't know. He's supposed to go there as well to visit ..." "Yes, yes, I know." " ... the entire situation, because there are all sorts of rumours ..." "Yes, yes, uh-huh." "He has to be here ... poor him. He really has the least time for himself. I'll tell him all that." "All right. If I call you from a different phone, then I'll just ask if he can bring that to me here so that we'd know theoretically if it is possible. And then we should agree about things." "Excellent." "Right. Give him my regards." "It was an honour speaking to you, madam." "Thank you very much."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, did you recognise any of the voices and the participants in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just recognised Biljana Plavsic's voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And were you able to follow the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, first of all --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware, at the time of this conversation on the 23rd of April, 1992, that Mrs. Plavsic was in direct contact with Arkan or Arkan's men?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. I do not recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let me ask you two things. Is that -- is the timing of the intercept generally familiar with your information about whether and when Arkan's men showed up in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just say this: Did the witness at all identify that this was Arkan? Do we know whom Mrs. Plavsic is talking to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the witness only said he recognised the voice of Biljana Plavsic. Just --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we are going on as if he had identified that she was talking to one of Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The other man, i.e., Rus, identified Arkan's first name during the course of conversation, did he not? Who is Zeljko, Mr. Mandic? Do you know Zeljko? Was it not the first name of Mr. Arkan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So do you confirm, then, Mrs. Plavsic was talking to one of the men of Arkan or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot, Your Honours. I had not heard -- I have not heard this conversation before this. I can only confirm that this is the voice of Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know approximately when -- whether -- first of all, do you know whether or not Arkan's men appeared in Sarajevo to fight on behalf of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this document be marked for identification before I move on to the next one, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if marking it for identification indicates that this witness has been able to make any foundation for this, we would object.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the witness has been able to make some identification, but I specifically asked for it to be marked for identification because I think there will be further evidence concerning this particular intercept, and I anticipate precisely that, in terms of its authentication. So I take Mr. Robinson's objection to some extent, but clearly the witness has provided information which will be part of that ultimate tendering for admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, furthermore, the witness identified the voice of Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. So, Mr. President, sometimes I'm a little confused, when we mark something for identification, whether that's some step where simply once intercept evidence is found to be reliable, all of the intercepts will come in without any further proof, and I don't think this should fall into that category. So to the -- maybe we're just agreeing. I don't understand exactly, but I just wanted to make the point that there would be some further evidence, in our view, necessary before this should be admissible, regardless of the question of authenticity of intercept evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The content of the conversation is related to a certain part of the witness's evidence, and the witness identified one of the voices, and the Prosecution is going to call a witness who will be filling up the gap. And what else? And when we -- at the end of the day, when we admit the marked exhibit for identification, we will consider all its circumstances comprehensively. On that basis, we see no problem in marking this exhibit for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be MFI P1106, MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn next -- thank you, Mr. President. If we could turn next to 65 ter 31679. This is a conversation between Mr. Prstojevic and Mr. Gagovic on the 14th of May, 1992. We may need to recommence that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Well, fuck, mistakes, you should not have made mistakes." "I know, but the men did not make mistakes. They were not ordered to--" "Leader?" "Hey!" "It is Prstojevic." "How are you?" "Thank God, I'm fine. If it weren't for this one mistake, I could be singing at the top of my voice." "Well, fuck, mistakes, you should not have made mistakes." "I know. We did not, but the men made mistakes. They were not ordered to do what they did." "Well ..." "Our movement is now a bit ... we cannot move with complete ... with that staff." "Sorry?" "Complete hardware is practically immovable right now." "Well, it is not my fault." "That means that is practically crossed out." "It is not ..." "Please, I have manpower, but I do not have the hardware now." "There is no ... he has manpower, but he does not have hardware. That hardware should not have been wasted, that is ..." "Where is that commander?" "Commander Popadic is there on the terrain, on the spot. At least two vehicles, two armoured personnel carriers should be replaced at this check-point." "Fuck it." "No crew, I do not need crew. I have the crew, I have everything. I have surplus manpower. That means ..." "Are APCs that arrived yesterday all right?" "Yes, the ones that arrived yesterday." "Is there a tank that is in working order? You should pull out those APCs. You should not let them fall into enemy's hands." "I do not know for sure if anything is in working order here. Two tanks, three APCs, and so on. I'm not sure for this check-point." "Fuck." "And those two yesterday are with Arkan's men?" "Where are they?" "They are probably -- there is no ammunition for one of them, probably ..." "Well, fuck, everything ... and where is that commander? I want to speak to him." "Okay. I will call him to get in touch with you. Let me just find him." "Have him call me." "Please." "Okay, bye."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Mandic, I think you've already indicated to us who Mr. Prstojevic is. Did you know who Mr. Gagovic was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know who Gagovic is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I refer to him as Colonel Gagovic, would that assist in any way?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By this time, mid-May 1992, were you aware that Arkan's men were in Sarajevo and working with Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tieger, this is the first time I see this conversation. I'm not sure. I cannot recognise any one of the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Just to be clear, are you disputing that it's Prstojevic's voice or you just don't happen to recognise it as you hear it in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tieger, I'm not disputing it, but I cannot recognise either one of the two voices.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mandic. And, Your Honour, I'd like that marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, I maybe should just note at this point that we don't think there has been any foundation whatsoever for its admissibility. But if you want to mark it for identification for some other purpose, you can do that. But following my understanding of the way we are proceeding, it shouldn't be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think any question was put to the witness as to the content of it, so let's admit it later on with another witness, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be clear on that, I think there was -- the conversation clearly refers to the presence of Arkan's men in Sarajevo, so I asked a question about Mr. Mandic's awareness at the time of that. This is clearly -- clearly arises from the subject-matter at hand, the invitation for Arkan's forces and other paramilitaries to come in, contemporaneous evidence of that, and I wanted -- so I'm not suggesting that this particular witness provides the specific authentication of the intercept via the conventional means of recognising the voices or participating in the conversation, but that when that happens, this will clearly be relevant to this examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You could have put that question without the document, and I don't think we need to admit this at this time. So we'll not admit this, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, okay. And, Your Honour, I'm not going to spend time -- I appreciate that. I have alluded to the possibility of discussing the nature of admissibility with respect to that. To give you an example -- well, let me just move on, and we can hopefully talk about that later. Thank you. If we could move on to the next document, 30724. This, Mr. Mandic, is a conversation conducted on the 15th of May, 1992, involving Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zugic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Hello." "Yes?" "Mico speaking. Who is that?" "I beg your pardon?" "Well, the Serbian MUP is calling." "Mico Stanisic?" "Yes." "Veljko Zugic speaking." "What's up, Zugic?" "SAO Romanija. How are you, Mico?" "What are you doing?" "Here I am." "I've been here for a month. Do send it from down there. I've just come from Sokolac, from the radio and television. Shut down." "Good." "Today we've been through, well, a lot of trouble." "Good. And where are you now?" "I'm in the Serb municipality of Ilidza." "Tell me what the situation is like ..." "With Vuk and Mlaco, with Prstojevic." "Tell me, what is the situation like over there?" "Well, we got reinforcement from Gagovic, some Arkan's and Seselj's men came, I don't know ..." "Good."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, do you recognise the voices of any of the participants in that conversation, either of the participants in that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
