utterances.text: I recognise the voice of Mico Stanisic, minister of the police.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask whether this is the entire conversation, or is there more?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, are you in the position to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, this is the entirety of the conversation that's ERN'd as the conversation on -- so the answer is, yes, Your Honour, in its entirety, in so far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't look like a finished conversation to me. It seems to have been edited, because the ending is not very logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not a proper intervention, Mr. Karadzic. Let's continue, Mr. Tieger. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you indicated in your Krajisnik testimony that you were aware of the presence of some Seseljevci in Sarajevo in April and May 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, in April -- or, rather, May, there were members of the Territorial Defence in Grbavica, the Territorial Defence of Nova Sarajevo, who were in the party of Vojislav Seselj. However, they were inhabitants of Sarajevo; that is, Brne Gavrilovic, who was born in Sarajevo, and he was in Seselj's political party. However, he belonged to the TO, the Territorial Defence of Nova Sarajevo. I knew of these men who were in Grbavica at the time. However, they are from Sarajevo, itself. From the point of view of their party affiliation, they are Radicals, but territorially they were from Novo Sarajevo. Gavrilovic was the leader of that small group. I can't remember his first name. His nickname was Brne, and he was born in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By mid-May -- did Mr. Stanisic expression concern to you in mid-May about the presence of Arkan's forces or Seselj's forces in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall, Mr. Tieger. There weren't any men of Seselj's. Vojislav Seselj was just bragging. He was turning his political party into an army. However, all of these people were from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they fought in the units of the Territorial Defence or the army. And he was claiming that these people belonged to them. Let me give you another example from New Sarajevo. At the Jewish cemetery, there was this man Aleksic. I can't remember his first name. Seselj kept saying that he was one of his men, but he was actually there providing security for the Jewish cemetery, and he was a resident of Sarajevo from before the war. It so happened that he had been born in Herzegovina, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mandic, are you disputing Mr. Zugic's comment as reflected in this intercept, that some Arkanovci and Seseljevci came and provided reinforcement along with Gagovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, Mr. Tieger. I'm not disputing it. Perhaps Munir Alibabic doctored this conversation somewhat. I don't know. In fact, I do not at all know who Nedeljko Zugic is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were aware that when Seselj's men were encircled on the 21st of April, 1992, that Seselj called to ensure that they be assisted in getting removed from that encirclement; correct? That's reflected in an intercept that you listened to, authenticated, and discussed in the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, those were members of the Territorial Defence of New Sarajevo, Nova Sarajevo. They had descended to Grbavica from Vrace, to the delimitation spot which divided the Sarajevo into the Muslim and the Serb part. They were members of Vojislav Seselj's Radical Party, but they were all Sarajevans, inhabitants of Vrace and Grbavica, and members of the TO of Nova Sarajevo. Now, what they called themselves, I know that they had a party leader which they all recognised, but I do know that Brne Gavrilovic was from Nova Sarajevo. He did not come there from Belgrade. He went to Grbavica from his own house in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn next to 65 ter 01601.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, it should be -- what the witness said, he didn't say -- he was by his home there, not he came there from his own house in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be looked into while editing the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just -- I'm not suggesting it's a particular problem in this instance, but maybe a more prudent protocol can be adopted for translation interventions. I think in previous cases, the protocol has been for counsel to identify the particular portion that's at issue and ask for some review by the translation unit, rather than, in the presence of the witness, provide a revised translation on the spot. Again, I'm not suggesting a particular problem in this instance, but I think it's probably a more prudent course adopt in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Points taken. Bear that in mind, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, 65 ter 01606. My apologies. It says "01601" in the transcript, and perhaps I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Return to e-court from Sanction?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, we should return to e-court. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, we'll be looking at a report to the minister of the Ministry of the Interior, dated the 10th of August, 1992, and I want to direct your attention to a brief passage on both page 3 in English and B/C/S, and at the top of both pages, which provide as follows: "It was stated, while inspecting the Pale Public Security Station, that a group of Arkanovci/Arkan's men/are still present at the Panorama Hotel. Chief Koroman presents that as a solved problem, because he is expecting their commander in a couple of days, with whom he would solve it without a problem." First, Mr. Mandic, let me ask you to identify for the Court what the Panorama Hotel was and who was generally present in the Panorama Hotel, what function it served during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Hotel Panorama at Pale was a hotel which is at Pale. I don't quite understand the question, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was it used for any official function? Did members of the Republika Srpska political or military authorities use that facility?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no, Mr. Tieger. The government used the Hotel Bistrica at Mount Jahorina, and the president of the Republika Srpska and the president of the Assembly were in a separate facility, the so-called Karadjordje's Inn. It is the so-called king's house, the royal mansion. On the ground floor was the president of Republika Srpska, to the best of my recollection. I don't know the exact layout. I know that President Karadzic later moved to the premises of the former Famos, and the Assembly members and the Presidency members were there for a time. And it used to be the king's house in a section of Pale towards Mount Jahorina, which they used for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We've seen previous references in both May and now here in August to the presence of Arkan within Sarajevo. Does that refresh your recollection at all, Mr. Mandic, about your awareness of Arkan's -- or the presence of Arkan's forces in Sarajevo in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I did not know that members of that paramilitary unit, the so-called Arkan's Tigers, came to the area of Sarajevo. I didn't know about that at all. As regards the so-called Seselj's men and Brne Gavrilovic, these were a group of Sarajevans from the Territorial Defence who were Radicals only in the political sense, but they had not come there from Serbia. They lived in Sarajevo. I know Gavrilovic personally. He is a Sarajevan. He was saved by the special police when he was encircled at Grbavica, and I had sent this special police to extract him from the encirclement. He had met several friends of his. Now, what they called themselves, whether they called themselves Seselj's men or something else, or -- I don't know, but Seselj is only associated with them politically, rather they with Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There's a limited amount of time left. So rather than get into something else, let me ask you one quick question and show you something very quickly. You said, in the course of your Stanisic/Zupljanin case, that it was -- referring to Mrs. Plavsic and, I gather, Dr. Djeric, and this is at page 9725, that these vain professor types did not realise what it means for people to go unchecked into villages, robbing and killing people and children. It seemed important for them "to have photographs taken with them." First of all, do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I held that opinion then, and I still do. I knew that General Mladic, the commander of the Army of the Republika Srpska, arrested these paramilitary units, and Mico Stanisic also arrested such paramilitary members, but Biljana Plavsic would intercede on their behalf and have them released, and then at Assembly sessions she should say how they did not allow our brethren over the -- across the Drina River, those from Serbia, to come and help their brethren here in their historical task. She was an authority, especially among the folk, among the plain people, but she created these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I just want to show you one video-clip and ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we do that tomorrow, Mr. Tieger? There are a couple of matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you going to tender that 1606 MUP report?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We would object to that. We don't believe the witness has spoken to that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To a certain extent, the witness confirmed the existence of some Seselj's men or Arkan's men, albeit in a qualified sense, did he not; Gavrilovic, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just looking at the part of the document that's on the screen, I don't see any reference to Seselj, but I do see a reference to Arkan, and I think he disavowed any knowledge of Arkan's men inside -- so for that particular document, I don't think he's confirmed any part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm a little confused by the position taken by the Defence, which is certainly contrary to what I thought was being urged before. Again, I distinguish this situation where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Mandic, you are free to go now. I'll see you tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask you, Your Honours, to be informed at least, in general terms, how much time I need to spend here more, I have to stay here? I've been here for seven days now, so how much more time is required by the Court, by the Prosecutor? If you could be so kind as to give me an indication, if that is possible, so that I can plan my own time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's try to find that out right now, to the best of my ability. Mr. Tieger, how much longer do you expect to have for your examination for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll certainly be completing it in the first session tomorrow, and probably well within the first -- in the first part of the first session, I anticipate, but within the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At most, about an hour, two hours. And we allowed about 20 hours at first, and so you can gather how much longer you have to stay here. But it may be subject to further changes. See you tomorrow morning. Thank you, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I cut it off in the middle, but have you completed your statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I just wanted to distinguish between circumstances where documents are brought to witnesses that don't arise from the examination, itself, or from the evidence provided by the witness. In this case, the witness talked about paramilitaries being invited in. I'm presenting him with official documents in this case reflecting the presence of those same paramilitaries. I think that's exactly the kind of position Mr. Robinson was urging on the Court previously. I appreciate the fact that he's trying to be consistent with what he understands to be some of the rulings that took place before. I actually think they are distinguishable on the basis of the fact that those were rulings made on documents that were presented to witnesses who weren't talking about those particular subjects, who were then presented with those subjects, and essentially being educated on those subjects. But I think, as a matter of principle, Mr. Robinson and Mr. Karadzic would prefer to see official documents come in in this fashion when they are raised in an appropriate context, as I believe they were here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As I alluded to that effect to a certain extent, the witness certainly commented upon the content of the document. As such, that can be admitted. So we'll admit that document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P1107.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With the indulgence --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something, just a word? The Defence was in a similar position when it dealt with documents speaking about the same phenomena that the witness spoke about. They were trying to refute what the witness was saying, and they were not admitted into evidence just because the documents were secret ones. Well, I have to express my dissatisfaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will do its utmost to apply the rule consistently and evenly. There are a couple of other matters. We'll come back to that Assembly session transcript later on. On 30th June, Mr. Robinson advised the Chamber that MFI D195 has been translated into English, and requested that it be admitted into evidence. Having reviewed the transcript of the 20th May 2010, when this document was used with Witness van Lynden, the Chamber is satisfied that it should be admitted, and orders that it now be marked as an admitted exhibit. Can we go back -- can we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's it for today. We'll rise until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 6th day of July, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.08 p.m.,
